Mr. SAM. SHARPE presented the fifteenth report of the Select Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Private Bills, as follows:
Your committee have considered the Bill No. 220 (letter U-3 of the Senate), intituled: 'An Act for the relief of Helen Vineberg,' and have agreed to report the preamble thereof not proven, on the ground that, in their opinion, sufficient evidence has not been adduced to establish the allegations set forth therein.
That the fifteenth report of the Select Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Private Bills he referred hack to the committee for further consideration.

Mr. Speaker, I desire to
say a few words on this question.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I would say that it is
not permissible to discuss the Bill at this stage. It is the report from the committee that is before us; the Bill is not before us; therefore hon. members cannot discuss the Bill, but can only give reasons why the report should otr should not be referred back.

Mr. Speaker, a few days ago I objected to the second reading of this Bill, and my objection was maintained on the ground that the proof in the case was not sufficient. We have not yet had the evidence laid before the House in French, and- we thought that the Rill would not come back to this House before the evidence was printed in that language. Yesterday I attended a meeting of the Miscellaneous Private Bills Committee, and the proceedings there strengthened my conviction that we should not proceed with this Bill. I maintain that we cannot form a sane judgment on this question without

seeing the evidence in our language. From what I have seen I am more and more convinced that this position should be maintained, and that we should have the evidence in French before any action is taken.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: When the hon. member raised his objection before, I inquired into the matter carefully and found that since 1885 the evidence on such Bills taken before the Divorce Committee of the Senate has never been printed in French. The question had been taken up in the Senate and at the request of the French members of the Divorce Committee a resolution was passed by the Senate that in future the evidence would not be printed in French. They did not think it desirable to have it printed, and from that time on the custom has continued. As to what would be required when the Bill reached this House and the Private Bills Committee of this House, that, of course, would be an entirely different matter, but I would regard the objection which the hon. member has taken as one of the strongest reasons for referring it back to the committee for further consideration, when it would be the right of any member of that committee to have the same witnesses called before it, to hear the evidence as it was given in the Senate, or to adopt any other method desired to obtain information with regard to the facts of this case.

I do not wish to delay the House, but I am bound to take exception to a statement made. My views on divorce are well known. I am opposed to divorce, -and think it should be abolished. That is the judgment of many people in this country. But, as regards the printing of the evidence; that is a matter of principle with me. Your honour states that a decision has been reached by a committee of the Senate by which the printing of the evidence in French is not required. This decision can only bind the Senate.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: That is what I said to the House. I stated that this decision could only bind the Senate, and, as it had no effect in this House, I gave no ruling on the subject.
Hear, hear.

There is no trouble about this. I have discussed the 'question with His Honour personally. I do not blame His Honour the Speaker for the view

he entertains. I take exception to His Honour's statement that to avoid the printing of a document in French a Bill could be referred back to the Private Bills Committee, where the hon. member for Ri-mouski (Mt. Boulay) and the other members of that committee would have a chance to have the witnesses brought before them, to hear their evidence, and to have that evidence translated into French if desired.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I said that it would be their privilege to have the evidence brought before them if they so desired, but I did not express any opinion as to the necessity of having printed in French the evidence which comes from the Senate. I simply said that this was one of the alternatives; but, as to the printing of the evidence in French, I expressed no opinion.

I hold the view that
any document coming before this House should be printed in both languages.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I understand that the motion is to recommit this Bill to the Private Bills Committee, which has already reported against it. There is a rule of this House, unwritten, but well understood, and I think a safe rule, that committees should toe supported by the House unless there is some very strong reason for the contrary action. Those of the denomination to which I belong do not believe in divorce, and we vote against it on religious grounds, and not upon the merits of each case. I hold as much as any one for the privileges of the French language in this House, but I do not understand the request which has been made by my hon. friend from Rimouski to have this evidence printed in French, because whatever may be the merits of the case he will vote against the Bill. There is no reason, therefore, why he should require the evidence to be printed in French. For my part, I do not read the evidence at all. It is bad enough that the English-speaking members who believe that the marriage tie can toe dissolved by Act of Parliament, and who are called upon to decide the merits of each particular case, have to read the evidence; but I am dispensed from that. Neither I nor the hon. member for Rimouski read the evidence. We shall vote against the Bill anyway, and therefore I cannot support this motion.

The right hon. leader
of the Opposition says that this Bill should
not be referred back to the committee unless for very good reasons. As the mover of the resolution, I will give the reasons why I ask that the Bill be referred back. My first reason is that the member for West Hastings (Mr. Porter), who has charge of the Bill, was unable to be present at the committee yesterday, as he was attending a sitting of the Supreme Court. Another reason is that owing to the House having sat till four o'clock yesterday morning there was a very small attendance of the committee, only seventeen of the sixty-four members voting on the motion to reject the Bill, which was carried by a majority of one. Another reason is that copies of the evidence had not been properly circulated; a large number of the members were without a copy. Another reasons that the Bill passed the Senate Committee by a majority of two to one. For these reasons, I think it is not unreasonable to ask that the Bill be referred back to the committee.

I am a member of the

of this House I desire to protest against this Bill being referred back for the reasons mentioned by the mover of the motion. The Bill was considered by one of the largest committees we have had this year, although several meetings have been held at which the Chairman required double sight to find a quorum. This Bill occupied the attention of the committee for nearly two hours, and was discussed at great length. The whole evidence was read and considered, learned counsel appeared for both parties, and in my judgment the committee would be establishing a very pernicious and dangerous precedent to grant a divorce on the evidence of one person, who had committed perjury over her own signature. For these reasons I submit that the Bill should not be referred back to the committee.

1 join with my hon. friend from Ottawa (Mr. Fripp) in protesting against the reasons that have been given by my hon. friend from Lanark (Mr. Tlioburn). The fact that the hon. member in whose name the Bill stands was not present at the committee is of no moment. He is not present this morning, and while the committee was sitting yesterday he showed so little interest in the matter that he did not trouble to attend. I agree with my hon. friend from Ottawa that it was a large and representative attendance of the

committee. Great interest, 'as shown in the proceedings, counsel for the petitioner and for the respondent were heard, and every part of the evidence was submitted and dissected by the committee, who deliberated over that Bill in all its disgusting details for an hour and a half. For what reasons does my hon. friend from Lanark move that this Bill be recommitted? Among the four reasons he gave to the House there was no hint of any new evidence, any new facts, or any new arguments. He simply expects that by some chance or mischance there may be a different attendance at the committee, larger or smaller, and hopes that there may be a different finding upon the evidence. I am not very much in love with the principle or want oi principle of divorce, but I have never voted with a clearer conscience than I did yesterday when this Bill was before the Private Bills Committee. It would be absolutely out of harmony with the principles of parliamentary procedure to recommit this Bill when it has not been shown that any injustice has been done, or that any advantage could be gained by so doing. My hon. friend from Lanark says that there was a very small attendance at the committee. Might I ask what greater attendance he expects at this stage of the session? This is Friday. If rumours are true and our expectations are realized, we shall arrive at prorogation early next week. Could a better attendance be got at the Private Bills Committee on Saturday, or on Monday, or on Tuesday, supposing the committee were to defer its sitting until then? 'There is one reason and one reason alone for the motion of my hon. friend from Lanark: it is that by a different attendance at that committee he hopes to get a different finding from the one arrived at yesterday. He says that copies of Ithe evidence .were inot cirflji-lated. Whose fault is that? If I take an interest in any Bill before a committee, as a member of that committee I am entitled to a copy of the evidence, and surely it is my fault if I do not complain; and I never heard a complaint yesterday morning in that respect- I venture to say that my hon. friend from Lanark will not -say that any complaint was made that the evidence was not circulated and in the hands of the committee.
The hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Bradbury) says that there was too much of it circulated. Possibly there was. One reason given by the hon. member for

Lanark why the Bill should be referred back is that it has passed the Senate committee twice. Why was it referred back to the Senate committee? It was referred back for the purpose of taking further evidence, it being contended that the evidence in support of the divorce as recommended by the Senate committee was not satisfactory. It was referred back, and was considered by the Senate committee, and that fact is not an argument to be used by my hon. friend from Lanark in favour of the recommittal of the Bill. The evidence upon which it was reported by the Senate committee on two occasions is the evidence which was before the Private Bills committee of this House; upon that evidence the committee saw fit to refuse to endorse the Bill, and with that decision I entirely agree. To ask now, at this late stage of the session, for a recommital is not in accordance with the principles upon which such matters are dealt with. I shall vote against it, and I hope that other hon. gentlemen will join me in that vote.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: When the hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) took the objection the other day that the evidence had not been printed in both languages, I was under the impression that the objection was well taken, and that the evidence should be printed in both languages. But I do think that the privilege of having two official languages recognized in this Parliament does not go so far as to have dirty . stuff printed in French for the purpose of circulation when we who belong to the Catholic faith believe it a matter of principle to vote against divorce anyway. I agree with what my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) has said in that respect, that no good purpose would be served by incurring the expense of having this evidence printed in French, and I would do everything in my power to prevent it from being circulated if what I have heard as to its character is correct. I am not taking any ground on the merits of the case, because I do not know anything about it. I think the Bill should be dealt with upon its merits, and I would not insist on its being printed in French. If it were, it certainly would be excluded from the mails as matter not fit to be circulated. I will vote against the motion for recommittal, not for the reason that the evidence has not been printed in French, but because I do not believe in divorce.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I do not know the merits
of this case, but it seems to me that it illus-

trates the .evils of the procedure by which divorces are brought about. As I understand this case, from the debate that took place a few days ago and from the debate this morning, the question as to whether or nf a divorce should be granted depends entirely upon the credibility of the witnesses. It further appears that all the members of the Senate committee, who heard the evidence and saw the witnesses, and the only member of the Commons who was present and heard the witness, believed those who were brought forward on behalf of the petitioner. It is usually considered that in the disposition of judicial affairs, the opportunity to see the witnesses, to hear them give their evidence, and to note their demeanour, assists in determining in a way not otherwise possible whether they are to be believed or not. Therefore, we have this remarkable condition, that those who heard the witnesses, without exception, believed the evidence of those witnesses who were called on behalf of the petitioner; and the members of the Commons committee, who, with but one exception, did not see the wit-*ppsrpr at all^ hftVA <l<?t0rEQiii6<I by s, majority of one-by a vote of nine to eight-that what was said by the witnesses ought not to be believed at all, and that a divorce ought not to be granted. Whatever may be said about the merits of this case, it seems to me to point to the conclusion that if applications for divorce are to be determined by the judicial decision of committees of the Senate and the House of Commons it would be a marked advantage if a joint committee could be arranged for, so that all those who are to determine the question in issue shall have an opportunity of seeing and hearing the witnesses. The present case does, in my opinion, show that the procedure is very unfortunate, very inadequate, and attended by a great many evils. I think it ought to be the duty of both branches of this legislature, in the early future, to consider whether or not some better mode of disposing of these questions could not be found.

The fact that divorce cases are tried, as they are, by the Senate, or Tather it is owing to that circumstance that we have this situation before us this morning, is a clear illustration of the necessity of changing the method, so that our divorce cases may be heard by the judiciary. As far as divorce proceedings are concerned, I have noticed since I have had a seat in this House, they are generally, or very often, decided not upon the
evidence as it is laid before the committee, and as they would be in a court of law; but those who have the decision in their hands are canvassed from day to day as to how they shall decide upon evidence that has not at the time been submitted to them. I do not propose to take up the time of the House, and I would not have risen except for the claim that was made by the hon. member who moved this resolution (Mr. Thoburn), as to the smallness of the committee.' As a matter of curiosity, last evening, after hearing that claim put forward in the lobbies, I had the matter looked up. I may say that I agree most thoroughly with the right hon. the leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) in the statement that committees of this House should be sustained and their reports upheld. That is customary, and it is good business; if we are going to quarrel with the decision reached by a committee every time a report is brought in, our work will be endless. The sitting of the committee yesterday was the largest that has taken place this year. There were twenty members present. The first meeting of the committee this year was on the 12th of February, and though there was not a quorum present, they did business. A quorum is ten, and there were eight present. SHARPE: I am a member of this committee, and it is my opinion that the Bill should be referred back for further consideration, inasmuch as many members of the committee did not have an opportunity of perusing the evidence. Members of the committee have told me that complaints were made at the sitting of the committee that the evidence had not been circulated. iMr. KYTE: We have reached a stage in this session at which all members are anxious to devote their attention to such important matters on the legislative programme as require our attention. speechtext: Order. I think the hon. member is going a little too far, because he is merely taking up the time of the House in discussing the evidence, which is not at present before the House.
I understand that the motion is to refer back this Bill to the Committee on Private Bills because there was insufficient evidence.
No.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I did not so understand. I understood that the principal argument was that the evidence had not been distributed, and that the members of the committee had not had an opportunity of reading it.

The motion of the hon. member for North Lanark, as I understand it, is that the Bill be referred back because there
was insufficient evidence to sustain the granting of the divorce, but I may be mistaken.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: That is not the question.

It is a matter upon which the committee were called upon to exercise judicial functions. The Divorce Committee i3 the only one required to exercise judicial functions in regard to matters that come before it. Therefore whatever may be the opinion in this House as to the weight that should be given to the reports of other committees, I think that, when a committee reporting upon an application for a divorce makes a recommendation to this House, this House is bound to accept that recommendation.

With all due respect
to the hon. member who has moved that this report be referred back, I desire to call the attention of the House to one feature of the case; and I do so more especially, seeing that my right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) has concurred in the view I have already expressed, namely, that our present system of granting divorces is eminently unsatisfactory. I do not think a better illustration of that unhappy state of affairs could toe found than in the case now before the House. We must bear in mind that when a motion such as this comes up, the Private Bills Committee having refused to pass the preamble of the Bill, and the rule of the House being, as I have always understood it, that prima facie the ruling of such a committee is binding and is to be upset only in case it can be clearly shown	that it	is wrong,
the respondent has certain rights, of which the House should hesitate to deprive him. I have no intention whatever of going into the evidence; but one fact is perfectly clear, namely, that two lines of evidence were given.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The evidence is not before the House; therefore it would be out of order to discuss it.

I stated that I had no intention of going into the evidence. I merely stated that two lines of evidence were given. Nobody will dispute that, a3 a matter of law, this House can grant a divorce on any ground whatever that may happen to appeal to the feelings of the members; but the uniform practice has always been that divorces are not granted except on the ground of adultery. That being the uniform practice of the House,

in a case where two lines of evidence were given, one wholly irrelevant to that practice, I think -the respondent has a double right, seeing that he has been attacked in such a manner as this, to appeal, as a Canadian, to his fellow Canadians for fair play. He has a right to do that, if the practice of this House is that divorces shall be granted only on the ground of adultery.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. It seems to me that the hon. member is practically dealing with the evidence, because he analyses it and says that there are two lines of evidence. The evidence is not before the House, and therefore it is not permissible to deal with it.
I am not dealing with the evidence. I am bound by your ruling, Sir, and I am not going into the evidence. I merely call attention to the fact that if two lines are taken-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I think in that regard the hon. member is out of order. He is analysing the evidence when he takes that position. My ruling is that it is not permissible to refer to the evidence.

I bow to your ruling, Sir, in that respect, although I had no intention of criticising the evidence or of going into it. I can say this, however, that this man, as a Canadian, has a right to justice from his fellow Canadians, and to appeal to every representative of the people of this country, of whom he i3 one, that his rights shall not be taken away from him.

What about the wife?
Is she not a Canadian?

The wife is certainly entitled, just the same as the husband:, to be protected. No one disputes that; but I say that, if the Private Bills Committee has reported against passing the preamble of thi3 Bill, then the respondent has the right to appeal to every member of this House, 'because, no matter what his religious views may be, he is sitting here as a representative of every man in Canada, not to violate his conscience by voting for anything he thinks wrong; but if, .having due regard to the evidence before him-I appeal to the hon. members for every province in the Dominion-he honestly believes that an injustice has been done to the respondent-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The hon. member is drifting back again into an examination of the evidence, which seems to me to be quite out of order.

Out of mere
eurosity and for the sake of a little information, I would like to know upon what principle it is not proper to dis'cuss the evidence upon this motion.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: For the reason that the evidence is not before the Houee. I take it that the House is concerned only with the question that is now before it.
Is it a fact that the evidence is not before the House?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Not at the present time.

The evidence was transmitted1 from the Senate to the House of Commons, and surely that evidence is officially before the House. My question was upon what principle members were not permitted to discuss the evidence on this motion. I desire to have the information, and I would like to have a ruling upon it.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The evidence was referred to the committee, and the committee dealt with it and reported to the House. The motion is that that report be referred back; and upon that motion, which is the only one before the House and of which the House can take cognizance, the evidence is not in question.

I wish to explain my position in reference to this Bill. I was a member of the committee; but, although I attended the committee yesterday in the determination to vote only in accordance with the evidence submitted, I was deprived of the opportunity of discharging my duty because the evidence was not placed before me so that I could intelligently vote thereon. As a member of that committee I understood that I had a right to a copy of the evidence in advance. I did not receive such a copy, nor had I an opportunity until afterwards of reviewing the evidence. I do not think that the whole evidence was placed before the committee in such a way as to enable each member to give a conscientious and consistent vote on the question before him. I had an opportunity of reviewing the evidence later, and I must say that the inconsistencies and incongruities displayed in it dissipated any doubt that existed in my mind. Therefore, had I been at that time



in possesion of the evidence, as I am now, my vote would have been cast upon the question; whereas, under the circumstances, I could not conscientiously vote one way or the other, and I accordingly declined to vote at all. Had I been in possession of the facts and been able to vote at that time, there is no doubt that the vote of the committee would have been reversed. I submit that the position I was in-and I understand that other members of the committee were in the same position, because there were others who did not vote-is a just and proper reason why this report should be referred back to the committee.

It has been propounded here by the right hon. leader of the Opposition and acquiesced in by hon. gentlemen who have followed him that it is a rule of this House, although unwritten, that the House must support the finding of a committee of the House. I have not long been a member of this House; but I think there is no rule, written or unwritten, to that effect. During the single session that I have been in the House, I have seen one Bill at least, the Bill respecting the Prudential Life Insurance Company, referred back to the committee after the preamble of the Bill had been defeated. Therefore, I think the House will not take very seriously the proposition that, after it has transferred to a committee of the House the power to deal with the subject matter of a Bill, it is bound to accept and acquiesce in the finding of that committee. I myself was not present at the meeting of the committee yesterday, and I have no right to claim any favour on that account; but, having read the evidenc'e, I, had I attended the committee, would have been bound to favour the divorce and would have done so. I concur in the view taken by many hon. members that the tribunal before which these divorce cases are heard is a wretched and miserable one.
Order.

I will modify that by saying that I think it is not in the proper sense a judicial tribunal; but it is the best one we have in some parts of Canada. One hon. member suggested that, this case having been-tried in committee, it should not be sent back again. This case has not been tried by the committee of this House. Whatever trial of a judicial nature there has been, has been before the Senate Committee. They alone heard all the evidence;

they alone were able to judge of the credibility of the witnesses as they gave their evidence, and they unanimously reported that Bill to the House. That having been done, the committee of this House did not try the case; they did not hear the evidence; they simply decided on the question, the evidence having been presented to some and not to others.

Owing to the absence of the Minister of Labour from the House through illness, the item in the Estimates relating to technical education was not reached. speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
My hon, friend will
remember that when it was proposed to the late Minister of Labour to appoint a commission to inquire into the conditions of technical education and industrial training in other countries as well as in Canada, apparently realizing that under the British North America Act education was one of the subjects exclusively assigned to the provincial legislatures, he communicated with the Prime Ministers of the various provinces to ask whether they respectively had any objections to the appointment of

such a commission. Replies were received from all the Prime Ministers to say that they had no objection to the appointment of such a commission. I may say that in writing them my predecessor stated that the only object of the commission was to gather information for the benefit of the different legislatures of Canada, that it was not proposed by the Government to go beyond that, but simply to gather information for the benefit of the legislatures. In their replies the several Prime Ministers expressed no objection to that course; -but the Prime Minister of Ontario and also the Prime Minister of Quebec in their replies said they had no objection to the appointment of a commission if it were distinctly understood that the commission was to gather information for the benefit of the various legislatures. My hon. friend from Pictou will know, having scanned the report of the commission, that -they went far beyond that, and not only gathered information in this country and in Europe tout made recommendations, which it was not understood they should do when the opinions of the various Prime Ministers were -taken. The latest volume of the report, No. 4, deals with the crucial point or 'question in the whole matter, that is, the condition of technical education and industrial training in the various provinces of Canada. That part of the report was not ready for distribution until some time in March of this year, although,'I had taken many steps to insist upon the report being completed long before. As soon as it was completed it was sent out to the various provinces with a request that they should express to us their opinions touching the report. We are in communication with the various Prime Ministers now. The Government, while having given the matter some consideration, have not reached a conclusion as to what course we shall take and will not toe in a position to reach such a conclusion until we have heard from all the local Governments in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I desire to say that
after giving the best consideration of which I am capable to the observation made yesterday by the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. 0'liveT), it 'appears to me that notwithstanding what he said it is desirable that this Bill should be enacted. I
think it is well that we .should not create a situation which may operate to discourage the taking up of homesteads by reason of the prolonged period required for naturalization. It is quite true that by reason of the amendment we made to the Naturalization Act, that prolonged period will not become necessarily operative for three years to come; tout at the same time it has been strongly urged upon me that it might operate to discourage the taking up of homesteads by persons after the first of January next, after the Act has come into force, toy reason of the fact that taking up their homesteads only after that Act had come into force they would have to comply with the five year period qualification in order to 'become British subjects. In deference to these views which are very strongly .and very generally entertained I think it is desirable to adhere to the original idea, and to pass the present legislation.

I can only repeat what I said yesterday, but I want to repeat and emphasise that I think a very, very serious mistake is being made by holding out the idea that free homesteads can toe -acquired without assuming the full responsibility of at any rate Canadian citizens, if not of British subjects having rights and responsibilities throughout the empire. I cannot -appreciate the point of view that considers the occupation of land the first essential in dealing wuth immigration, and that the great purpose is the -arrival of people and the cultivation of the land. These purposes are only means to -an end, and that end is the eetatolishment of desirable citizenship. I think it would be very unfortunate if, for any reason, the Government were diverted from that view, which has been accepted from the very toeginning of the dealings of Canada in regard to free homesteads in- the West. It has been -a rock-toottom principle, and while I appreciate the difficulties in combining the requirements for imperial naturalization with the local requirements in regard to homesteading, if they cannot be combined, if one or the other has to go, then I say by all means looking at the matter from the Canadian standpoint and from the imperial standpoint it is better that we should insist on Canadian citizenship as a condition of acquirement of land at the hands of this country than that we should forego Canadian citizenship for the sake of establishing imperial citizenship.

I want to refer to the argument that has been so prominently put forward in the press and by responsible people in eastern Canada and in the United Kingdom. They hold that there is a danger of the alienation of western Canada from the ideas of British citizenship, and that there is a serious danger to the Dominion and to the empire in adherence to the principles and ideals of our civilization. I believe that under conditions as they have existed up to the present time, that view has been unduly exaggerated; but it has a measure of sound foundation, and the proposal of the Government in this legislation gives it form and body and weight such as it never had before. I want to repeat that the whole purpose of our policy of increasing our population by immigration and of bringing under cultivation our vacant lands, is not merely to increase the number of people living within the bounds of Canada and to increase the number of bushels of wheat that may be raised or exported, but it is for the purpose of establishing a stronger, because more numerous, Canadian citizenship, not without but with the ideals that we believe accompany that citizenship today; and the first and greatest responsibility of this or any other Government of Canada is to adopt such measures as may be right
and	reasonable,	as	may be	fair	anddo	justice to	all	parties	concerned,	to	ensure as	far	as possible	thatCanadian ideals	shall be	built	up
and Canadian citizenship strengthened. The first means at hand to do that is to hold out to all the world: We give you certain advantages under certain conditions; we do not ask you to come to this country to be hewers of wood or drawers of water for other people, but we ask you to come here to take part with us in the opportunities we are able to give you for building up the civilization and conditions that we already have established. I am for immigration, and I am for increasing the material development of our country, but I am not for immigration or for increasing the material development of our country unless thereby we build up a Canadian and an imperial citizenship and Canadian and British ideals of civilization.

I usually agree with the logic of my hon. friend from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver), but on this matter I think his logic is absurd. I do not think that his views will be very largely shared by the inhabitants of western Canada. As far as I can see-and I listened to my hon.

friend's speech yesterday as well as to-day -he fails to make two very necessary distinctions to arrive at a proper conclusion. He mixes up citizenship with what is in its essence a purely commercial undertaking. I do not think it has been in the minds of most Canadians that when they offer homesteads they do so, in the first instance, with the view of making citizens of the British Empire. It is with the view of developing the commercial interest of Canada. That is the primary duty of any Government in this country. In nine cases out of ten the people who come to this country with the object of taking up homesteads come with the object in view of increasing their material prosperity. They come to Canada because Canada is a good country to live in. Coming to Canada, I am inclined-from a considerable and intimate experience of homesteaders from many other countries-to believe that they find that their material interests run in the direction of still higher interests, and, in the case of our American friends as well as others, they become attracted to our laws and to the country, and in the end become citizens. I think my hon. friend has failed to draw a distinction between the grounds on which citizenship rests and what is purely a commercial undertaking whether on the part of the individual homesteader or on the part of the Government which arranges the conditions under which he shall homestead. There is another distinction which I should have thought would have occurred to the mind of my hon. friend. He is making a distinction without saying that he is doing it, or at least he does not seem to indicate that he is doing it. Is it a fair thing to a homesteader to ask him to be a citizen in order to own 160 acres of land while another American can come in an buy 10,000 acres of land without any question being asked? I see very little in the contention of my hon. friend at all, and I think the latter consideration would sway my thought on the matter. The fact that any person can come in from anywhere, buy 10,000 acres of land, leave the country or live where he likes, would lead me, in a sort of fairness of spirit, to recognize that the commercial undertaking of the homesteader is a significant factor in the development of the country, and I have a sufficient knowledge of the effect of the privilege of citizenship upon people who come to Canada to be able to assert that the result is, as I have already stated, that in nine cases out of ten the homesteader i.'lti-

mately becomes a citizen. If you make it compulsory that the homesteader has to become naturalized to get his homestead, he naturalizes in this country, gets his homestead, then goes back to the United States and renaturalizes there and you lose your citizen. The citizen who is worth having is the one who takes a higher view of citizenship than the mere possession of 160 acres of land.

The view which my bon. friend has put forward is absolutely contrary to what has been accepted by every Government of Canada and by the people of Canada ever since they have been dealing with homestead laws.

I am afraid
that my hon. friend is a Tory when he gives suca a reason as that.

I can always Change for
the better but not for the worse. When a certain principle has 'been maintained for such a long period of time, when it is held 'by the Government that is putting through this legislation and when, in so far as we have been informed by the Government, it i3 a sound principle, when, contrary not only to the principle of former Governments, but of this Government, we are asked to adopt (this legislation, surely it ought not to be put through without the attention of the	country being called to it.
We objected to the legislation that this is complementary to. We have been insisting upon certain requirements in order not only to attain imperial citizenship,; but the best Canadian citizenship, and while we are doing that on the one hand, we are establishing a new condition contrary to the accepted principles of every Government that has preceded this one and of this one itself. I would not delay the House at such length on this question if I did not deem it to be as important as it is. I have had to deal in many capacities with many people who have come to settle in our western country. All nationalities who come to settle carry with them the natural instinct of love and reverence for the country of their birth, and there is a natural tendency to re-establish in the new country the conditions of the old. Bn some cases this produces desiraJble results, but it is also true that in other cases it produces undesirable results. Looked at in the light of the experience that I have had and the problems that we have to face, the very first duty of the Government is to establish in the minds of all people who come here to share with us the opportunities of this country that the opportunities of Canada involve the responsibilities of Canadian citizenship and that we, who have opened up and are developing this country, are offering these opportunities to the people of the world for the definite purpose of building up and strengthening our nationality and our ideals, and not for the purpose of changing, or of altering, or, if you like, degrading that nationality and those ideals. When the Government sees At to change that policy which has been pursued during so many years for a certain definite purpose, without any reason having any bearing upon the principle at all,
I say it is a serious matter; and the minister is not well advised in reconsidering his opinion of yesterday that the amendment might very well be left over for another session. The whole idea of our naturalization legislation as expressed by the minister was to make naturalization m Canada dear, to make it important, to make the alien realize that he was acquiring something that was of serious value to him. But by this legislation, he lets the alien know that Canadian citizenship is not a serious matter, it not a matter of value. He destroys the very purpose that he has in his naturalization legislation with the very people with regard to whom it is most needed.
Bill as amended reported, read the third time, and passed.

Hon. W. T. WHITE (Minister of Finance) moved that the House concur in the amendments made by the Senate to Bill No. 70, respecting Trust Companies. He said:
The amendments are not of much importance, and I see no reason why they should not be concurred in. The title of the Bill is changed by adding the figures ' 1914 ' making it read 1 The Trust Companies Aet-1914 '. Section 3 is changed as to its phraseology, making it more clear. At page 6, line 18, a sub-clause is added providing that in case an election of directors is not made the company shall not be held to be thereby dissolved. That is not an unusual clause in company legislation. Then at page,9, line 15, there is provision to the effect that notwithstanding the forfeiture of shares for non-payment of calls,

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: the shareholders shall continue to be liable to the creditors of the company for the full amount unpaid on such- shares at the time of forfeiture. There is no objection to that provision, eo far as I can see. At page 20, there is a somewhat important amendment, but in my view it is an improvement to the Bill.

The Senate usually
makes improvements.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Sometimes it does; it is certainly within its right in taking into consideration Bills of this kind and improving them if they are susceptible of improvement. I must say that in Bills originating on this side of the House, particularly those under my own charge, there is but limited potentiality of improvement.

But the Senate has improved this one.
Mr. WHITE; Slightly. By section 63 it is provided that trust funds held by the company may be invested:
In the stock, funds, or Government securities of Canada or of any province of Canada, or guaranteed thereby respectively, or bonds, or debentures, of any municipal corporation in any such province
To this, in the Bill, there was this exception :
-other than municipal corporations having a population of less than 2,000 or an actual rate of taxation exceeding two cents on the dollar exclusive of school tax.
The Senate has struck out that exception. I understand that representations were made to the Senate by bond dealers to the effect that the exception involved a discrimination against the securities of many municipalities of not quite 2,000, population, but which in the future would have many times 2,000. It. was also urged that it was not well that the rate of taxation should be made the test of the quality of a municipality's securities because by the simple expedient of raising the assessment the disability could be overcome, and so a premium would be put upon increasing assessments. I should say myself that the proper test is rather the indebtedness per head than the rate of taxation or the population of a municipality, and therefore I agree that, while this is a comparatively old exception, it migiht well be struck out. Under the section as amended, trust company funds may be invested in:
-the stock, funds, or Government securities of Canada or any province of Canada, or guar-
[Mr. W. T. White. 3
anteed thereby, respectively, or bonds Or debentures of any municipal corporation in any such province.
The other powers of investment conferred upon the company by the section are continued as they were when the Bill left this House. There is one other minor addition. The Senate has added the debentures of school corporations as well of school districts which were authorized under the terms of the Act as it stood. On page 25 there is a verbal change from ' this ' to * the.' These are the amendments which have come from the Senate and I think this House should concur in them.
Did not my hon. friend tell the House when he introduced this Bill that it should not be made retroactive?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
What I said when the Bill was being introduced was in answer to a question asked by my hon. friend, and it was to the effect that I was not in favour of retroactive legislation except when it was clearly necessary in the public interest. My hon. friend in asking the juestion, had in mind the case of trust companies which had been incorporated either by specia} Act or under the provisions of the Companies' Act,	with wider	powersthan	he-and	I	also thought	shouldbe	granted	to	such compabies.He	referred	particularly to	those
companies which had not yet been organized. The Bill as I introduced it in the House was not retroactive in the sense that it would cut down the powers possessed by any trust companies which had been heretofore incorporated, but certain sections of the Bill-those relating to the powers of the company to create preference stock and issue share warrants, as to the meeting of shareholders, the mode of keeping accounts and the return of annual statements, provision for inspection, provision for penalties for valuation of the provisions of the Act-all these were made to apply to all companies heretofore incorporated. I thought at the time that no exception could be taken to making these provisions retroactive because they did not in any way cut down the powers of these companies.
It was not-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
It seems to me not
regular at this stage to enter into a general discussion of the Bill. There are now before us for consideration the amendments

made by the Senate only. A general discussion of the Bill is irrelevant.

I think there is another section that is made retroactive, section 66, -which provides for the investment of the companies' funds. That is made retroactive and might -work to the disadvantage of the company.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: It is out of order to discuss sections of the Bill that are not before the House for consideration. The subject under consideration is simply the amendments made by the Senate. There is a growing habit of late, when the House is in Committee of the Whole, to let the debate go backward and forward indiscriminately, without regard to the natural order of procedure, and it would seem to me that an effort is being made to follow the same bad custom when not in Committee of the Whole.

If these amendments are to be considered, would they not have to be referred to committee? I would like my hon. friend to consider in that connection, so that no time would be lost, the bringing of this Bill into operation on the 1st of September. That would give trust companies time to get rid of their real estate under the limitation of the section.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the matter is of some importance, perhaps by consent, even though somewhat irregular, I might be allowed to give an explanation to my hon. friend. Section 66 is made retroactive on and after the 1st day of January, 1917. Section 66 refers to the investment powers of trust companies. In the Banking and Commerce Committee, subsection 7 of this section, as it now appears in the Bill, was introduced, and the report of the committee was adopted in this House. _That subsection provides:
The provisions of this section shall, on and after the 1st day of January, 1917, apply to all trust companies heretofore incorporated under the Companies Act or by special Act of the Parliament of Canada.
So, these companies have until the 1st day of January, 1917, to dispossess themselves of any investments they may have that are not in keeping with the provisions of this section. Now, I understand that the matter was brought to the attention of the Senate, and that this section was fully considered by a special committee of that House. .It was subsequently adopted by the Senate, I believe, on the
report of that committee. -So that the Bill, as reported from this House with no amendment to section 66, was adopted. I understand that one or more trust companies were represented before the committee of the Senate, and pointed out that they would be unable to carry on the business which some of them are now carrying on, namely, dealing in lands and at the same time carrying on a trust company business. I think the remedy which was suggested to them, though I speak with reserve as to that, was to make application to the Secretary of State under the Companies Act to change their corporate powers and divest themselves of their trust powers, in the event of their electing to continue dealing in lands, and carry on a business which if carried on by a trust company would be in contravention of this section 66. I understand that an amendment is being prepared by the Minister of Justice to the Companies Act, which will enable companies of this character to make application for a reduction of their powers. At present, under the Companies Act, while there is provision for the enlargement of powers, for the supplementing of powers already possessed, there does not seem to be any provision for the curtailing of powers which have been conferred upon companies incorporated under that Act. The Senate has made amendments in this Bill, but it has not made amendments in this section. I, do not see that the amendments made are objectionable, and therefore I move that they be concurred in.

I am afraid that my hon. friend does not quite understand the force of the objection that has been raised. Certain members of the Senate think that it is an oversight not to provide that the Act shall come into operation at a future date. One of them spoke to me on the subject. I am not sure that I fully understand the point, but I understand that it is thought desirable to allow trust companies time to bring themselves under the requirements of the Act by carrying on a trust business solely, and to take advantage of the proposed amendment to the Companies Act before this Act comes into force.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I had verbal information that that was the view held by at least one member of the Senate. Personally I do not see any objection to providing that this Bill should come into effect on the 1st of September or the 1st of October next, but it is not possible under the rules for this House now to insert a provision of this

kind. I find that Bourinot, referring to this stage of a measure, says, at page 677:
Neither House can regularly, at this stage, insert any new provision, or amend, or omit, any part of a Bill it has itself passed and sent up to the other House for concurrence. But it is perfectly in order to propose any amendment to an amendment made by the one House to a Bill of the other House, provided it is consequential in nature; that is to say, consequent upon or relevant to the amendment under consideration.
I would be perfectly willing to insert a section in this Bill providing that it shall not come into force until September 1, 1914, but such an amendment would not be consequential upon the amendments which have been proposed by the Senate, and under the rules we can do nothing but concur in or amend consequentially the amendments which come from the Senate. I discussed the matter referred to by my hon. friend with the Minister of Justice this morning, and his view and mine, upon looking at the interpretation clauses of the Act, is that if a trust company desires to take advantage of the new provisions in the Companies' Act and to make application to have its powers cut down so that it shall no longer be a trust company, it would not then be subject to the provisions of this Act, which are made retroactive. In other words, this Act would only apply to it so long as it continued to be a trust company as defined under the interpretation clauses of this measure. I think that that is a correct view, and, therefore, I do not see how any inconvenience will arise. If by chance such inconvenience should arise and be brought to my attention, the proper method, in my judgment, of dealing with the matter would be to introduce a Bill next session declaring that the retroactive provisions of this Act shall not apply to companies which take advantage to the Companies' Act of the amendment to which I referred, so as to make it perfectly clear that the retroactive provisions apply only to trust companies so long as they continue to be trust companies as defined under the interpretation clauses of this Act.
Amendments concurred in.
