speechtext:
On motion of Hon. W. T. WHITE (Minister of Finance) the House went into Committee on Bill No. 185, for the relief of the depositors of the Farmers Bank of Canada, Mr. Blondin in the Chair.
On section 1-short title:
You are not going to make the title general, and come to the relief of depositors in all bank failures ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am afraid that would not be an apt title.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 2-payment of depositors in Farmers Bank:
This section refers to section 131 of the Bank Act and speaks of ' the holder of any charge upon the assets of the bank.' Whom would that include' P

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The first charge on the assets is in favour of note holders; next come governments, federal and provincial; and then depositors and other creditors. This section excludes note holders and any

governments having a charge upon the assets of the bank. For instance, the Ontario Government would be excluded.
Had it a deposit in the Farmers Bank?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

In my opinion, the
ordinary creditor of the bank has just as good a right to be reimbursed as the depositor. A case has been recently brought to my attention of a gentleman who drew through his own local bank for a certain amount on a debtor in the province of Ontario. Subsequently the draft, without his knowledge, came into the hands of the Farmers Bank, who presented it and received the money a few days before the failure of that institution; and the owner of the money appears to have lost it. In my judgment, he has an even better claim to be reimbursed than the depositors. A depositor is a lender, and these depositors lent their money to the Farmers Bank because it was paying a higher rate of interest than other banks. The ordinary business man when he sends a draft into his own bank does not know where it will go. He does not know the connections of the bank with whom he is doing business, and he relies on the banking institutions of the country; and in my judgment he has a stronger claim than the depositor whd simply lends his money to the bank.
Has my hon. friend any evidence to show that any branch of the Farmers Bank paid a higher rate of interest than other banks?
No more than what I have heard stated in the course of this debate.
My information is that it did not pay a higher rate of interest.
If the statement is not correct I wish to withdraw it, but I heard the statement made by several speakers in the course of the debate. I have no personal knowledge of the matter.

I have been trying to find out from some hon. gentlemen who had branches of the Farmers Bank in their constituencies whether the Farmers Bank really paid a higher rate of interest than other banks. I have made inquiries of the hon. member for Durham (Mr. Thornton), and the hon. member for South Huron (Mr. Merner), and they both inform me that while such a report was in circulation
the branches of the Farmers Bank in their constituencies paid exactly the same rate of interest as other banks.

That may or may not be true. However, it makes no difference to my argument. I was saying that the depositor is a lender, and that these depositors selected the Farmers Bank as the parties to whom they would lend their money, and that in my judgment the ordinary creditor of the bank has a better claim, equitably, than the depositor. I have not heard this point raised during the course of the debate, and I would like to know the views of the Finance Minister on this matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If I understand my hon. friend rightly, the party who has the claim to which he alludes is not a depositor. This Bill is to relieve the depositors who had money on current or savings account in the Farmers Bank. There are creditors other than depositors. Other banks in Canada hold drafts, money orders, and certified cheques on the Farmers Bank amounting to |14,000.
Are they to be paid?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No. This Bill provides merely for reimbursing the depositors.

If the reason assigned
by the hon. Minister of Finance for the passing of this Bill is a good one it is applicable to every creditor of the bank just as well as to the depositors. Why the depositors should be singled out to be repaid the money they deposited in the Farmers Bank as against all the other creditors of the bank I cannot understand. The reason given by the minister as a justification for the passing of this Bill is ostensibly that the Treasury Board of the former Government was negligent, and improperly if not wrongfully granted a certificate to the bank to do business. If that is the case every creditor of the bank is entitled to be paid as well as the de. positors. If it is not the case then the depositors are not entitled to be paid. I must enter my protest against the passing of this Bill for the reason assigned by the Minister of Finance unless he will include among the parties to be paid every creditor of the bank. If the Treasury Board negligently and wrongfully granted a certificate, then every creditor of the bank is on a footing of equality with the depositor. A depositor has no more right than an ordin-

ary creditor simply because he sees fit to deposit his money in a bank. It is asserted that the Farmers Bank paid a higher rate of interest than other banks. I am authoritatively told that they paid one per cent more than any other bank in the locality. It has been stated by hon. members representing constituencies in which that institution had branches that they did pay a higher rate of interest on deposits than other banks did. If the reason given by the Minister of Finance is a good one for the payment of any creditor then that reason should inure to the benefit of all the creditors the same as it does to the benefit of depositors.

The riding which I represent had two branches of the Farmers Bank with deposits amounting to about $120,000, and I can positively say that three per cent was all these branches paid, not four per cent.
I would like to ask the Minister of Finance if he has ever made any inquiries as to the rate of interest that was paid by the Farmers Bank branches on deposits?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have never made any specific inquiry. My understanding has been that they paid the same rate as others but I am not certain as to that, because I have not made any inquiry.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. Postmaster General (Mr. Pelletier) favoured us the other day, with an admirable statement of the situation as regards the Farmers' Bank and other banks. Nothing could be said further that would give us a clearer insight into the question.
I have carefully gone over the speech delivered by the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. White) when the resolutions concerning the Farmers Bank were introduced. I also read through a return brought down in compliance with an order of the House of Commons dated January 16, 1911, and included in volume 45, No. 24, of the sessional papers for 1911. I have also read through the report of Commissioner W. R. Meredith, dated Fehruary 21, 1913, concerning that same bank. But that report reminds me somewhat of a fair maiden who having two lovers and been anxious to retain them both, arranged to have them call on different days.
It would appear from the statement of the hon. Minister of Finance, based on the 
report of Commissioner Meredith, that we are bound to grant relief to the depositors who have suffered enormous losses through , the failure of the aforesaid bank. True, in that report, at page 8, I read:
My conclusion on this branch of the inquiry is that the Treasury Board was induced to give its certificate by false and fraudulent representations on the part of Travers, and that if the facts I have mentioned as to the way in which the $250,000 was made up had been disclosed, the certificate of the Treasury Board would not have been given.
It is plain from the letter of the Finance Minister to Travers, of 30th November, 1906, that the Minister understood that section 13 of the Bank Act would not have been complied with if the $250,000 was made up wholly or in part of money raised on promissory notes given by subscribers for shares to the provisional directors and that he would have felt it his duty to recommend that the certificate should not be granted if he had known that part of the money had been raised in that way.
Obviously the Commissioner was anxious to exonerate the Treasury Board and the Minister of Finance for having issued, on November 30, 1906, that certificate which enabled the bank to start business. But what strikes me as most peculiar in that report of the investigating commissioner is the statement to be found a little further on:
That that information had been given to the minister before the certificate was issued appears from the testimony of Sir Edmond Osier and Mr. David Henderson and is shown by the letter of the 19th October, 1906, of Mr. Leighton McCarthy to the minister,.
I do not suggest that the minister would have been justified because of the information conveyed to him in recommending that the certificate should not be granted, or that the Treasury Board because of it would not have been justified in refusing to grant it, but, having received the information, it was in my opinion incumbent on the Treasury Board to have investigated the charges that had been made before coming to a conclusion as to whether or not the certificate should be given.
It will be seen that, in this instance, the Commissioner blames the Treasury Board and the Minister of Finance. But further on he endeavours once more to exonerate them. Indeed, at page 9 of the same report, will be found the following statement :
And the most that can properly be charged against the Department of Finance or the Treasury Board is an error of judgment.
Now, I fail to comprehend how the investigating Commissioner was able to reach the conclusion that there was committed a mere error of judgment in this whole business, when he says at page 8 -in a previous paragraph:
Although the information which had been conveyed to the minister had evidently im-

pressed him with the necessity for further inquiry on his part before advising- that the certificate shall be given, the only inquiry made was that contained in his letter to Travers, of the 30th November, 1906.
In my humble view, that simple letter, far from relieving the Minister of Finance of the heavy responsibility of inquiring into the facts brought to his attention by Messrs. McCarthy and others, further incriminates him, and shows conclusively that there was not only committed a simple error of judgment but that the ex-minister of Finance showed a quasi criminal neglect of the public interests confided to his care. That whole report tends to exonerate the Minister of Finance and the Department, especially when it is stated at page 10:
I am unable to find that there was any neglect of duty on the part of the department, or to see that anything more than what was done could have been done, even if Mr. Vankough-net's letter had stated, which it did not, that the promissory notes he referred to were notes that had been given in respect of shares included in the list furnished to the department when the application for the issue of the certificate of the Treasury Board was made.
It follows therefore that in two different places the investigating commissioners blames the former Government and in two places exonerates them as well.
I for one, do not find the conclusions of the investigating commissioner to be in agreement with the fact disclosed by the correspondence between Travers and the Finance Department,- previous to the issuing of the aforesaid certificate. In the first place, I am not called upon to express an opinion in respect to the conduct of Travers and the shareholders; the hon. Minister of Finance has gone fully into that last evening. The whole thing is a series of unprecedented frauds, and a scandalous exhibition such as should never ibe given by people who aspire to command the confidence of the people. I do not propose to read the whole correspondence and to draw the conclusions which flow naturally from the letters exchanged between the parties interested, that is to say Travers and the Department of Finance. However, in order to understand how the matter stands, it is necessary to look into that correspondence.
In the first place, it will be necessary to read a letter dated October 8, 1906, addressed to the hon. W. S. Fielding by L. McCarthy and which reads as follows (page 1 of the Sessional documents):
Toronto, Oct. 8, 1906.
Hon. W. S. Fielding,
Minister of Finance,
Ottawa.
My dear Mr. Fielding,-I have been consulted
on behalf of a number of subscribers to the shares of the Farmers' Bank, and from the instructions I have received a number of the subscribers will dispute the bona fide character of the subscriptions. I have not time to-night to give a full statement of the grounds of this request to you, but I beg to assure you that grave conditions have arisen which will require careful consideration before the Treasury Board would grant any certificate for the organization of this bank.
I therefore ask you to be good enough to stay any action which might be taken until 1 have had an opportunity of discussing this with you. If it is not asking you to hold it too long, I would prefer not having to go to Ottawa this week, but will go any day next week which would suit your convenience. Of course if there is no immediate prospect of your granting such a certificate my seeing you at an early date will not be necessary.
Leighton McCarthy.
The wording of that letter was sufficiently clear, not only to give rise to doubts in the mind of the minister as to the regularity of the organization of the Farmers' Bank, but, moreover, to induce him to be very cautious and even to investigate all suspicious circumstances previous to issuing the certificate. It was followed by a message dated October 11, which reads as follows:
Toronto, Oct. 11, 1906.
Hon. W. S. Fielding,
Minister of Finance,
Ottawa.
Please wire me assurance in reference to stay of certificate of Treasury Board mentioned in my letter of Monday night.
Leighton McCarthy.
And pray observe that the aforesaid letter was written only fifty days previous to the issuing of the certificate enabling the bank to start business. The minister acknowledges receipt of Mr. McCarthy's message in the following words:
Ottawa, October 11, 1906. Leighton McCarthy, M.P.,
Toronto.
No application yet received for the certificate referred to. Please forward your representations immediately and they will be considered when application comes.
W. S. Fielding,
Minister of Finance.
Now, he admits at the time that no request has as yet been made, but that he is on his guard, and in a letter bearing the same date as the aforesaid message, he lays further stress on the statement herein contained:
Minister of Finance, Canada.
Ottawa, October 11, 1906. Leighton G. McCarthy, Esq., M.P.,
Toronto.
My dear Mr. McCarthy,-I have your letter of the 8th instant, and your telegram to-day on the subject of the Farmers Bank.

I wired you to-day that no application had been made by the promoters for the Treasury Board certificate, and suggested that you send forward at once any representations which you may wish to make, to which we shall give all due consideration.
W. S. Fielding,
Minister of Finance.
To which Mr. McCarthy sends the following reply on October 12:
Toronto, October 1?, 1906. Hon. W. S. Fielding,
Minister of Finance,
Ottawa.
My dear Mr. Fielding,-Many thanks for your telegram received last night, advising me that no application had yet been received for certificate of the Farmers Bank and asking me to forward representations immediately when they will be considered. This will receive my attention.
I am obliged to you for the telegram.
Leighton McCarthy.
But all that precedes is nothing in comparison with the following letter from Mr. McCarthy dated October 19, that is to say, only forty days previous to the issuing of the required certificate. That letter is so plain and based on such firm grounds that, after reading it, no Minister of Finance could ever issue a certificate without laying himself open to the charge, not only of lacking in judgment, but also of showing a culpable, if not a criminal neglect. The! letter reads as follows:
Toronto, Oct. 19, 1906.
Hon. W. S. Fielding,
Minister of Finance,
Ottawa.
Re the Farmers Bank of Canada.
My dear Mr. Fielding,-1 beg to inclose the special endorsement upon a writ of summons in the High Court of Justice for Ontario, which will be issued by William A. Saxon, John Sproat, George Castle, William McLean, Finlay Mc-Callum, Robert Hume, James Murray, George Denoon, John McLeod, Jane Shuert, William Harris, on behaf of themseves and all other persons alleged to be subscribers for shares of the capital stock of the Farmers Bank of Canada wTho may desire to come in and be parties to this action, against the Farmers Bank of Canada, James Gallagher, John Watson, John Ferguson, Alexander Fraser, Alexander Shepherd, Lown, W. R. Travers, C. H. Smith, A. G. H. Luxton, and the Traders' Bank of Canada, and W. J. Lindsay and I respectfully request that the Treasury Board will stay any action upon the application of persons professing to act in the name of the Farmers Bank of Canada, or in the name of the provisional directors of the Farmers Bank of Canada, for a certificate under section 15 of the Bank Act on the grounds alleged in the inclosed special endorsement, and other grounds which may be disclosed upon the examination of the alleged subscribers for shares.
I have received information that the alleged subscribers for shares paid a large sum of money in cash and have signed notes for other large sums of money, and that the persons pro-

fessing to act in the name of the bank have transferred notes and received the proceeds, and that a deposit either has been made or will be made of the cash received and the proceeds of these notes, or sufficient amount to make up $250,000.
I wish you to have the kindness to acknowledge the receipt of this protest against the granting of a certificate so that I may advise the shareholders who are disputing their liability, and I would be pleased to go to Ottawa upon any appointment you may make for the further consideration of this matter.
Leighton McCarthy.
What a strong worded protest is served on him on behalf of a responsible advocate of the city of Toronto, and forty days after the minister allows the issuing of a certificate enabling this bank to start business, notwithstanding the charges which are made against it; and Mr. Meredith's report is content with stating that there has been committed an error of judgment! To my mind there is more than that, there is carelessness, remissness, if not intentional forbearance with a view to defrauding the public. And the aforesaid letter was duly received at the Finance Department, for on October 23, that is to say four days later, an answer was sent to Mr. McCarthy, which reads as follows:
Department of Finance, Canada,
Ottawa, October 23, 1906. Leighton McCarthy, K.C., MP.,
Toronto, Ont.
Dear Sir,-I beg to acknowledge the receipt of your letter of the 19th inst. to Mr. Fielding's address respecting the Farmers Bank of Canada. When application is made by the Farmers Bank to the Treasury Board for a certificate to enable them to commence business, the representations contained in your leter with its enclosure will be laid before the board.
(Sgd.) T. C. Boville,
For Deputy Minister of Finance.
On the same day, Travers wrote also, and the dates are so close, that it is not possible to suppose there was an oversight on the part of the Department of Finance. The letter from Travers reads as follows:
The Farmers Bank of Canada,
Toronto, Oct. 23, 1906. Hon. Minister of Finance, and Receiver General of Canada,
Ottawa, Canada.
Dear Sir,-I hereby beg to enclose you certificate No. 1150 from the Bank of Montreal, Toronto, for $250,000, to be deposited to the credit of the Farmers Bank of Canada in compliance with section 13 of the Bank Act.
Please acknowledge receipt and oblige.
(Sgd.) W. R. Travers,
General Manager.
On October 24, that is the day following that on which they had written to McCarthy, an acknowledgment was sent of the papers received from Travers:

The General Manager,
The Farmers Bank of Canada,
Toronto.
Dear Sir,-I beg to acknowledge the receipt of your letter of the 23rd instant, enclosing receipt and draft of the Bank of Montreal, Toronto, for the sum of $250,000 deposited by your bank in compliance with section 13 of the Bank Act.
I may say in this connection that opposition has been filed in this department to the granting of a certificate to your bank under section 14 of the Bank Act.
T. C. Boville.
To which Travers replied as follows in a letter dated October 29:
Toronto October 29,1806. The Hon. Deputy Minister of Finance,
Ottawa, Ontario.
Dear Sir,-Yours of the 24th, post-marked October 26, was received here on the 27th.
I was surprised to know that any one had filed an opposition against this bank being granted a certificate.
Would you kindly do me the favour of supplying me with a copy of the said objections, ""as I do not know up to the present moment wherein we have deviated in the slightest effect from the Bank Act.
W. It. Travers,
General Manager.
I quote herewith another letter dated October 31, addressed to Mr. McCarthy, and signed Boville, which shows furthermore how suspicious the department had become in respect to the Farmers5 Bank of Canada.
Dear Sir,-Referring to your letter of the 19th instant, addressed to Mr. Fielding, on the subject of the Farmers Bank of Canada and the issue of a certificate to that bank to commence business under section 15 of the Bank Act, I noticed recently a reference in the newspapers for a judgment given by Judge Anglin in a suit relating to this matter. In view of the decision rendered, I shall be obliged if you will let me know if you still desire the protest contained in your letter to be brought before the Treasury Board upon an application of the Farmers Bank for a certificate to be considered.
T. C. Boville.
Now, on that date of October 31, that is to say, exactly one month previous to the issuing of the certificate enabling the bank to start business, a certificate granted on the application of Travers, the protest is still in the hands of the Deputy Minister, and there is enough anxiety felt over it to induce the officials to inquire from Mr. McCarthy whether he still proposes to submit the matter to the Treasury Board when the time comes to consider the application. Why bother their heads about that protest, if it was not of some importance? Why should they worry about it? Indeed it was because that certificate was of a nature to arouse suspicion in respect to the organization of the said bank, and that is further evidence that the enabling certificate should never have been issued without a thorough inquiry being made.
On November 2, a copy of McCarthy's protest is transmitted to Travers as follows :
Ottawa, Nov. 2, 1906.
W. R. Travers,
Toronto, Ont.
Dear Sir,-I beg to acknowledge receipt of your letter of the 29th instant, and in reply I beg to enclose herewith a copy of a letter addressed to Mr. Fielding by Mr. Leighton McCarthy by way of protest to the granting of a certificate to your bank to commence business. Of the enclosure with Mr. McCarthy's letter I have not sent you a copy as it is lengthy, and I have no doubt you already have a copy of it in your possession.
(Sgd) T. C. Boville.
True, Mr. McCarthy, on November 2, writes the following letter withdrawing his objections:
Toronto, Nov. 2, 1906. The Hon. W. S. Fielding,
Minister of Finance,
Ottawa.
Dear Sir,-Referring to my letters of the 8th and 9 th instant, with reference to the application for a certificate made on behalf of the Farmers Bank ; I am advised by those who are instructing me that the claims made by them in the action brought have been settled by their subscriptions being taken up by some parties interested in the bank and refunding the money paid by the individuals or returning the notes which had been given. The objections which I made on their behalf to the issue of the certificate are therefore withdrawn. Would you mind therefore returning to me the papers which I forwarded to you.
(Sgd) Leighton McCarthy.
That was only twenty-eight days previous to the issuing of the certificate, and the minister, notwithstanding the withdrawal of Mr. McCarthy's protest, is open to blame for not having inquired into the whole transaction before taking so great a risk, which has had such disastrous results for those unfortunate depositors and even directors, if they are called upon to-live up to the double liability clause. The Hon. W. S. Fielding, Minister of Finance in the Dominion Government, to whom had been confided the guardianship of the public treasury, trusted by his party and by the government, having in his responsible position the supervision of the finances of the Dominion, was bound to be the more prudent that ha was in possession of a higher post of public trust. Any blame that the former minister is open to, as a consequence of that unfortunate transaction, does not fall on him personally, but as the official representative of the govern-

ment, who is responsible towards the public and bound to compensate those who have been shamefully robbed.
On November 21, we havs a further letter from Boville to Travers, which reads as follows and shows that the importance of the information supplied had not been overlooked :
Department of Finance, Canada,
Ottawa, Nov. 21, 1906. W. R. Travers, Gen. Manager,
The Farmers Bank of Canada,
Toronto, Ont.
Dear Sir,-Referring to your letter of the 23 rd October, making a deposit under section 13 of the Bank Act of the sum of $250,000. X have no doubt that you will be applying very shortly for a certificate under section 14 to commence business. In the papers to be submitted to the board in support of the application there is a list of bona fide subscribers of capital stock of the bank showing subscriptions to the extent of $500,000. Would you be so good as to have added to this list for submission to the board, a statement showing the actual amount of cash paid up by each subscriber.
(Sgd) T. C. Boville, Deputy Minister of Finance.
The CHAIRMAN of the COMMITTEE (Mr. BLONDIN: (Translation.) Will the hon. member allow me to inquire whether he proposes to discuss the whole bill?
Mr. BOULAY. (Translation.) No.
Mr.	BLONDIN.	(Translation.)	We ars
sitting in Committee of the Whole, and I think the hon. gentleman should postpone his remarks till the third reading of the Bill. I take the liberty of calling the hon. gentleman's attention to the fact, as I would not like to take the responsibility of allowing a general overhauling of the Bill at this stage of the proceedings.
Mr.	BOULAY.	(Translation.)	I	wish
simply to lay before the House some viry interesting documents in connection with this matter, so that the public may be in a position to form an opinion. Besides, I have only a couple more letters to read.
Mr.	GAUVRliAU. (Translation.)	And
those documents are so new!
Mr.	BOULAY.	(Translation.)	On	November 27, we have a letter from Travers to the Deputy Minister of Finance, enclosing the documents required under the Bank Act (page 7):
The Farmers Bank of Canada.
Toronto, Nov. 27, 1906. To the Deputy Minister of Finance,
Parliament Buildings,
Ottawa, Ont.
Dear Sir,-I have the honour herewith to forward declaration of the general manager

of the Farmers Bank of Canada setting forth facts relating to the incorporation and organization of the said bank, and also giving the names of the directors elected at the meeting of subscribers and such other particulars as are required by the Bank Act. The provisions of the Act as to subscriptions and deposit with the Receiver General having been fully complied with on behalf of the said bank, I apply for the certificate of the Treasury Board permitting the said bank to commence the business of banking.
(Sgd) W. R. Travers,
General Manager.
On November 28, Mr. Boville forwards to Mr. Newcombe thi record in the matter of the Farmers' Bank (page 28):
Ottawa, Nov. 28, 1906.
E. L. Newcombe, K.C.,
Ottawa.
Dear Sir,-I beg to forward you herewith a return of the application of the Farmers Bank of Canada in connection with the granting of a certificate enabling it to start business under sections 13-17 of the Bank Act.
Kindly let me know whether such documents justify the issuing by us of said certificate.
The following is Mr. Newcoinbe's answer, dated the same day, giving his opinion: Ottawa, Nov. 28, 1906.
To the Deputy Minister of Finance,
Ottawa, Ont.
Sir,-I have the honour to acknowledge receipt of your letter of the 28th instant, and of the inclosed papers, being the application from the Farmers Bank of Canada for a certificate to commence business,- under section 13-17 of the Bank Act, and papers in support thereof.
You ask me to advise you if on the papers submitted such certificate may legally issue.
In reply, beg to state that the statements in the statutory declaration of Mr. Walter R. Travers are sufficient, if they are accepted, to show compliance with the statutory provisions and that the evidence thus afforded is such as the Treasury Board may lawfully accept under the Act, and thereupon issue to the bank a certificate under section 14 of the Act.
Papers returned herewith.
E. D. Newcombe.
Two days after, on November 30, the Hon. W. S. Fielding writes to Travers the following letter which, not only excites some suspicion, but arouses very grave doubts in my mind:
Dept, of Finance, Canada,
Ottawa, Nov. 30, 1906.
W. R. Travers,
Genrl. Manager Farmers Bank of Canada, Russell House, Ottawa.
Dear Sir,-I regret that owing to pressing engagements yesterday, arising out of the Budget, I was unable to meet you to consider your application for the issue of a certificate to authorize the Farmers Bank of Canada to commence business. I shall be glad to see you to-day, at my office, at any time before one o'clock if you can call. Or I might be able to see you later, between four and five, at

the House of Commons, if that will he more convenient.
There is a phase of the matter which I should like to bring- to your notice so that you may consider it at once. It has been represented to us that in some previous instances where an application was in all respects apparently regular, there was actually an evasion of the intention of the Bank Act in relation to the paid-up capital. We have been told that in some cases the subscribers did not actually pay in cash but gave notes to the provisional directors which were used to raise the money. On account of information of this kind, which has reached us in relation to a previous case, we deem it proper to scan very closely every application for a certificate which comes to us. I shall be glad to have an assurance that nothing of the kind has taken place in relation to the subscriptions for the Farmers Bank, but that the amounts set forth in the application as having been paid up have in every case been bona fide cash payments.
W. S. Fielding,
Minister of Finance
The contents of this letter plainly show, not only that the minister had some doubts, but that he knew almost to a certainty that the deposit of $250,000 required under the Banking Act of Canada had not been legally effected; and should there he only that letter in the whole record, it constitutes sufficient and overwhelming evidence not only of carelessness and neglect, but, so to speak, of extraordinary forbearance under the circumstances towards the notorious manager of the Farmers Bank. And to satisfy his timorous conscience, which current gossip had somewhat perturbed and disquieted, the hon. gentleman was content with having an interview with his personal friend Travers, and a mere verbal explanation on his part is considered sufficient to justify the issue of the desired certificate so long expected and which was required to enable the bank to start business. On a mere letter of Travers, written, no doubt, after that five hours' interview, and on that same day, perhaps at that very hour, though it was already late, on that 30th day of November, possibly at six o'clock in the evening, the certificate was issued, and Travers departed quite elated at his success in this connection.
However, on that same day, November 30, in a letter which is included in the return, Mr. E. S. Clouston was already protesting against the organization of the Farmers Bank; but little heed seems to have been paid to it by the Finance Department. His letter was answered, but Travers, notwithstanding his extortions, his false reports, his false dividends and his false entries, succeeded in keeping the bank afloat until the month of December, 1910, when the catastrophe occurred which had long been expected and which the Finance Minister of the Laurier Government had contributed in bringing about. To-day we are called upon to pay the price of the faults, the carelessness, not to say the complicity of that Government, in one of the worst financial schemes which has been unloaded on this country.
Therefore, I express the opinion that the former Government through the medium of the ex-Minister of Finance, have laid themselves open to blame in issuing that certificate enabling the bank to start business, the effect being to lead people erronously to believe that all was right and that they could safely make large deposits in that bank, deposits which they never would have made if they had been in possession even of the meagre information which the department had in hand. For the department had been notified of the manoeuvres of Travers and the directors. Previous to the issue of the certificate. Travers could not start business, but once the certificate issued, the public saw no reason to withhold its support from an undertaking thus endorsed by the Dominion authorities. Under the circumstances, and after considering the statement made by the Government, I declare myself favourable to the proposal of reimbursing the deposits made in that bank.
I may be allowed, Mr. Chairman, to read a complete list of the banka which have failed in Canada since confederation. The hon. Postmaster General has given out the names of a certain number of these banks; but there are a few missing which I would like to include. I shall add a few particulars as follows, in respect to the date on which business was suspended, the amount due to the people, the payment of bank notes and deposits, as well as the total amount of the doss inflicted on the people:

speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 4-payment:
Is it intended that this money shall be reserved for the widows and children and shall not be available for the creditors of the deceased depositors?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is the intention.

Upon what principle? If the losses had not been incurred by the creditors of the bank, such deposits
CM. Boulay.]
would have been available at law to the creditors of the depositors. You are rather changing the character of the assets.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The payment to the depositors under the authority of this Bill is not a legal liability on the part
4 p.m. of the Government, although the matter has been argued on the analogy of legal principle. We thought it proper to provide that, in the case of death of a depositor, the money which would otherwise be paid to him under this section, should be paid to his widow and children and should not be exigible at the instance of his creditors. I suppose my hon. friend is strictly logical in saying that, had the bank not failed, the money would have been available to the creditors; but I do not think there will be any serious objection to the course here proposed.
You are making it a pure gift by putting in that provision-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It is a gift to the dependents.
Mr. MACLEANwhereas the purpose of the Bill is to restore the original financial condition of the creditors in relation to the bank. It seems to me you are not carrying out the purpose of the legislation. I do not think that the speeches made by the Minister of Finance and other hon. gentlemen

opposite contemplated such a disposition of the moneys to be paid out of the consolidated revenue account as is proposed. I think it is altogether a new idea.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There is legislation upon
the statuteJbook of Canada under which money, to which a party or parties may be entitled, may be by the Government handed over to the widow and children, as we propose to do here. I know what is in the mind of my hon. friend. He thinks that, if we proceed logically upon the assumption that the Government is bound to reimburse these depositors, there is no reason why the creditors should not be protected in regard to the rights they have to the deposits so restored; but as I pointed out, there is no such legal liability upon the Government in this matter. We have argued it on the ground of legal analogy, and we think the Government is morally hound to make reparation. No objection has been taken to this provision except on the part of my hon. friend.
