speechtext:
Section agreed to.
Bill reported.
The Hon. W. T. WHITE (Minister of Finance) moved the third reading of the Bill.

Will the minister furnish us, at the beginning of the next session of Parliament, with a list showing the names and descriptions of the persons and the amount paid under this legislation? This Bill does not provide for that, and I do not suppose any other statute does. It might be well for Parliament to have this information.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not see why such a
return should not be made; and if by any chance it is overlooked, if my hon. friend will move for the return, I think I can promise him that the information will be brought down. Parliament is undoubtedly entitled to it.
Does the Government intend to take any steps to recover the moneys which have been paid out illegally by the bank?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That will he the duty of the liquidator. If my hon. friend has any information which is not at present before the liquidator, I shall be glad on receiving it to forward it to him. I have no knowledge of any such payments, but it is quite possible, even probable, that there were such. If so, I have no doubt the liquidator has 309J
given the matter attention, as he is a very competent man.

Before the Bill is read the third time, I wish to he permitted to move an amendment. In the discussion which took place the other day, the hon. Postmaster General threw out a hint that similar applications would be received in the cases of other failures of banks throughout the country. This was also referred to by my right hon. friend the Prime Minister, who said that, if there were any other cases that came under the same principle, they would be considered by the Government. A number of other cases have been referred to in the course of the discussion, such as the Mechanics Bank at Montreal, the Bank of Liverpool, Nova Scotia, tlhe Bank of Prince Edward Island, La Banque Ville iMarie, and other hanks. In the case of La Banque Ville Marie, it has been drawn to the attention of the Government by my hon. friend from Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) that there was gross negligence on the part of the former Government in not attending to the inspection of that bank and in not insisting on proper returns being made under the banking law. In the case of the Bank of Prince Edward Island, it was drawn to the attention of the Government, by questions asked by my hon. friend for Kings, Prince Edward Island (Mr. Hughes), that in that province at the time the province came into the union there were five small banks doing business. Two of them had a capital of about $100,000 each, and the others had a smaller capital. No provision was made in the Act bringing the island into the union as to what would be the fate of those banks that were carrying on business in that province at that time.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member is rather wandering away from the question before the House, namely, the third reading of this Bill. It appears to me that it is not permissible to go into the principles of other banks and banking, and I think the hon. member ought to address himself to the question as to whether this Bill shall be read the third time now
The amendment I intend to move deals with the whole question, and I think your honour will see that I am perfectly regular in the remarks I intend making.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Then it would perhaps be better if the hon. member would send

up his amendment or read it, so that the Speaker could have some idea in regard to the matter.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Is it your ruling, Mr. Speaker, that on the third reading of a Bill the principle cannot be discussed as on the second reading?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: No. My ruling is that the Bill can be discussed, but that the discussion of other and extraneous matters having no direct relation to the Bill is out of order. The third reading is the proper time for the Bill to be discussed and a motion made to amend it, if desired.
I was referring-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Would the hon. member send up his amendment?
I wish to make my argument before I submit the amendment.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
But the Speaker could
deal more intelligently with it if he had the amendment in his hands.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Even if my hon. friend has no amendment to propose, can he not discuss the Bill?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: He can discuss the Bill on the third reading. But, if I understand the hon. gentleman correctly, he is dealing with banks and banking back to Confederation, including matters that, so far as I can see, have no relation to this Bill. With regard to the amendment which the hon. member proposes to make, my suggestion was that if that amendment were in the Speaker's hands the Speaker would know whether the hon. gentleman was addressing his argument to that amendment or not. The amendment might give a latitude which the Bill without the amendment would not give.

If I am free to discuss the Bill without an amendment, surely I am free to discuss it with an amendment. I understand Your Honour to say that I am free to discuss the principle of the Bill and to discuss it as freely in that sense as on the second reading. I will endeavour to keep myself within that ruling.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Perhaps the hon. member scarcely apprehends my meaning. An hon. member in addressing the House must address himself to the last question propounded before the House. In the case of an amendment he would be at liberty to deal with what was contained in the

amendment as well as what is contained in the main motion, which would give him wider latitude than he could have on the discussion of a motion for the third reading of a Bill. That was my object in desiring to add the amendment-that I might know whether the hon. member was keeping within the limits of the amendment and of the Bill itself.

I have no objection to show Your Honour the amendment. At the same time, I wish to address myself to the principle of this Bill, and to make the remarks that I was prevented from making, at the instance of the chief whip of the Government, on the occasion of the second reading. Perhaps Your Honour will remember that before the end of that discussion the hour was very late. It was necessary that the Prime Minister should be allowed to speak. It was understood between myself and the chief whip of the Government side that if I withdrew on that occasion I should be allowed to deal with the question as fully as on the second reading. I understand that is the position I am in now. I would point out also to Your Honour, that my hon. friend from Rimouski (Mr. Boulay) a few minutes ago made a speech referring generally to the whole subject matter of the Bill.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: If I might be allowed to interrupt-I think there would be no wisn to curtail the scope of the hon. gentleman's remarks.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Personally I have no
objection. But I might say that I was present during the consideration of the Bill in Committee of the Whole and the discussion was not at all in regular order. Under the rule, in Committtee of the Whole, a member speaking must address himself to the clause under consideration. But the discussion wandered over the whole Bill and other questions as well. I only wish to keep the House to the usual parliamentary business lines of discussion, which are pretty well understood; it is not my desire to curtail anything which the hon. gentleman has a right to say.

I should be very sorry
to do anything contrary to the ruling of the Chair. I have the greatest respect for your' Honour's opinion. But I scarcely understand why I should not be allowed to discuss on the third reading everything contained in this Bill. As I understand

that you have permitted me to go on, I will continue my remarks.
I was pointing out that at the time Prince Edward Island came into Confederation these banks were in operation, in that province. There was no Treasury Board in Prince Edward Island and no possibility of the existence of such an institution., under the local government of that province, after the province came into the Union. The [DOT] federal Government assumed charge of the banking laws. Apparently it was the duty of the federal Government to have some sort of supervision over these banks. But the banks were allowed to continue in business at their own sweet will, and to issue notes without any supervision, either on the part of the local government which had no jurisdiction, or on the part of the federal Government which had jurisdiction, but failed to exercise it. The consequence was that one of these banks, known as the Farmers Bank, and another, known as the Bank of Prince Edward Island, failed, and, I understand, the depositors lost a large amount of money. The fact was drawn to the attention of the Government, through questions .asked by my hon. friend from Kings, P.E.I. (Mr. Hughes), that that state of affairs existed in Prince Edward Island, and the Prime Minister having suggested that it was open to the depositors who lost money in any part, of Canada to make a similar claim to that made by the depositors of the Farmers Bank, I thought it was necessary that an amendment should be moved that would put the country in possession of the information with regard to these other institutions in which money has been lost in a similar way.
Now this measure is important, in view of the fact that it involves a new doctrine in Canada. The doctrine that has prevailed in this country since Confederation, and in the provinces of Canada prior to Confederation, is ' The King can do no wrong '-that the government of the country is not responsible for. a mistake made by a minister or officer of the Government. That is the doctrine that has always prevailed in this country and in the old country as well. And I submit that it is a good doctrine. We have always had a great deal of faith in the administration of the Department of Finance in Canada. Other departments of the Government on certain occasions have been besmirched with scandal, but I do not recollect that on any occasion during the history of Canada since Confederation,
there has been suspicion that there was anything crooked or wrong in the administration of the Department of Finance. That department has been managed during that period by very illustrious men. In looking over the names, I find that the department has been under the direction of such distinguished men as Sir John Rose, Sir Francis Hincks, Sir Richard Cartwright,. Sir Leonard Tilley, Sir Charles Tupper, the Hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Foster) and the Hon. W. S. Fielding. I submit that there is not one of these statesmen, who have been honoured with the portfolio of the Department of Finance, who would have been willing to stand as godfather to the illegitimate proposal we now-find on the table of the House. I have said that we are establishing a new precedent in Canada;-may I add that it is a vicious precedent and that there is absolutely no justification for it?
We hold the present Finance Minister responsible for a transaction of this kind. The old-fashioned notion is that the Finance Minister is the guardian of the consolidated revenue of this country, but, having regard to his conduct on this and other occasions during the present session, it looks to me as if he were developing into a kind of modem Robin Hood, with ithis difference: that Robin Hood seized the property of the rich and divided it among the poor, while my hon. friend seizes the property of the taxpayers of this country, and hands it over to em-barassed millionaires and political friends.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Such as the depositors of the Farmers Bank.

I submit that this legislation establishes a vicious and dangerous precedent and that we should not adopt it. We are tending to acceptance of the principle that a license issued by the Government involves the assumption that the persons to whom we issue that license are honest and straight, and will use properly all the powers given to them by that license, and that it is the duty of officials to ascertain this before issuing the license. I submit that that principle will apply to many other things, as well as to banks. The Secretary of State day by day is issuing charters to joint stock companies to do business in this country. The same provisions which relate to banks are found in the law relating to companies. It is necessary that the parties applying for a charter to do business as an incorporated company shall put up a certain amount of capital;

that a certain amount shall be subscribed nnd a certain amount paid in. The law, Therefore, is the same in this particular dn respect of joint stock companies as in [DOT]respect of banks. But does the Secretary [DOT]of State make any investigation with a wiew to ascertaining whether the capital so subscribed is borrowed or whether it is taken out of the till of the subscriber? No such thing; he vannot do it. A solicitor comes to his office with an affidavit similar to that made in this case, in which he states that the law has Deen complied with; he produces also a certified check for a certain amount of money. Every solicitor in Canada who has had anything to do with these matters knows that all the Secretary of State asks for is the statement of the solicitor or some reputable subscriber that the company is regularly organized. But we are adopting a principle under which we go farther, and if it turns out that any of these companies are improperly chartered; that the amount of the check is made up of money paid in for the purpose of obtaining a charter and that there is no real capital behind the company at all, we make ourselves just as liable in that case as we do in the case of banks. I admit that we ought to take greater care in the case of banks, but what I do say is that the principle is the same and if the Government is to be held liable for issuing a license in the one case, it ought to be held liable for the consequences of issuing a charter in the other.
A few days ago the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries introduced a Bill changing the law relating to pilots on the St. Lawrence river. Prior to this date the pilots were licensed by a pilotage commission. In future the pilots will be licensed by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, and it will be his duty to select competent men. Suppose that a man whom he had selected upon a supposedly good recommendation of competency was put in charge of the Empress of Ireland and was responsible for the collision that took place in the St. Lawrence whereby $2,000,000 worth of property and many lives were lost, what would be the consequence? Would not the persons who sustained these losses come to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries and say: This man was licensed by your department; you committed an error of judgment in licensing the incompetent or drunken man who was responsible for the wreck of this ship; consequently you are liable for the loss. A few years ago 
I submitted a claim to the late Government in regard to the loss of a schooner containing a valuable cargo on the coast of Nova Scotia. The circumstances were these: There was a sunken ledge off the port of Whitehead in that province; this ledge could not be seen at high tide and only in case of a storm could the breakers be observed. The Government for a great many years had been placing a buoy to mark the location of that sunken ledge, and prior to the occasion to which I refer a Government steamer placed a buoy fifty yards inside instead of outside the ledge, where it should have been. As a consequence, while endeavouring to round the buoy and make the port, a schooner carrying a valuable cargo struck the ledge and the schooner and cargo were lost. The Government gave me the usual answer, that the King can do no wrong; that the Government provides these aids to navigation free of charge and that consequently the Government was not responsible. They turned up some cases where claims of that kind which had been made against the Department of Marine and Fisheries had always been rejected on that ground. I had to accept the position, because I knew that that was the law, although this was a case wherein very great hardship was involved. Serious mistakes like that may occur, and it is easy to describe them as errors in judgment, as in the case now before the House.
The question of the character of Mr. Travers has been discussed by gentlemen who have spoken on this subject and it has been stated over and over again by supporters of the Government that Mr. Fielding ought to have discovered that Mr. Travers was a dishonest man. Let me ask, who suspected Mr. Travers at the time he approached the Finance Minister for this license? Was not Mr. Travers at that time a man of good reputation? Was he not known to be a successful business man in the province of Ontario? There is not a hint in the evidence that any person ever raised a question as to Mr. Travers' character until long after that date. The hon. member for Halton did not say anything reflecting on Travers' character. He does not say that he told Mr. Fielding that Mr. Travers was dishonest. If he did know anything that would justify such a statement, I feel certain that he would have made it known to Mr. Fielding. The hon. member for Halton has never been afraid to speak out in meeting. He was always an able and energetic critic when he was in oppo-

sition, and if he had a case against the late Government he would be the first man in the House to stand up and state it. The hon. member for Halton did not think that there was anything very serious wrong with Travers' character or he would have taken more action than he took on that occasion. The hon. member for West Toronto (Sir Edmund Osier) did not make any suggestion to Mr. Fielding that there was anything wrong so far as Mr. Travers' character was concerned. He seems incidentally to have expressed a pious opinion that it was not wise to license this bank because it was going into the hands of inexperienced men and into the hands of a board of directors who did not know very much about the banking business. That appears to be the substance of the warning given by the hon. member for West Toronto. At that date the hon. gentleman was a prominent director of the Dominion Bank. The Dominion Bank was a member of the clearing house in Toronto. The clearing house does not need to admit any disreputable man to membership. We fail to find that the hon. member for West Toronto took any objection to Travers. It is said the bank rather welcomed him at the time he applied for admission to the. clearing house, showing that the hon. member for West Toronto did not himself think that there was anything very bad in this case, or he would certainly have taken some action to prevent Travers from joining that association. The case of the Bankers' Association is a little different because automatically a chartered bank comes under the Bankers' Association and has a right to join it, but that does not apply to Bankers' Clearing House Association. So, when the hon. member for West Toronto failed to make any objection to the admission of the Farmers Bank as a member of the clearing house, I say that he failed to do his duty if he knew there was anything wrong about Travers. Then it was drawn to our attention that Colonel Munro, one of the prominent men of Ontario, a man who on two occasions had been a member of the local legislature of that province, whose character was very high, who was a private banker, who was well known in all of that part of the province of Ontario to be a man of very good character and of high integrity. How is it that Colonel Munro did not discover that Travers was a scoundrel, if Mr. Fielding ought to have known it when the charter was issued? Why is it that Colonel Munro afterwards became an associate of
Travers and agreed to become president of the bank that Travers shortly afterwards wrecked? If Colonel Munro could not find him out and the four or five hundered other shareholders, respectable citizens of Ontario, did not discover it; if they met year after year and elected him as director and continued him as general manager of the bank, if in all that time no person found, out that Travers was dishonest, how could it be expected that Mr. Fielding could have found it out when Travers applied for the license at the Department of Finance?

What did the writ issued
by Mr. Leighton McCarthy and served on Mr. Fielding mean?

I do not regard that ap a very important matter. The writ wag served by parties who were dissatisfied with the way in which the bank was being financed, but the writ was withdrawn and the Department of Finance was notified that it had been withdrawn; not only that, but in the notice that came from Mr. McCarthy to the Finance Minister it was stated that other parties had taken up the stock. What more could the Finance Minister want? He did not care who had taken up the stock so long as it was taken up. It was assumed, of course, that Mr. McCarthy meant, and any person would assume he meant, that the stock had been regularly subscribed for by somebody else, and while those who had owned it retired from being shareholders, other shareholders had come in to take their places and that, it appears to me, made the matter all right. How was it that two years after the bank was organized the Hon. Matbeson, the treasurer of Ontario, deposited the money of the province with Mr. Travers? Surely if there was any place where Travers would be known it would be in Toronto, the capital city of the province of Ontario, where he resided. But the provincial treasurer of Ontario had such confidence in Travers that he deposited the funds of the province with him nearly two years after the date on which Mr. Fielding issued the certificate. All these facts make it very unreasonable for hon. gentlemen to say that Mr. Fielding ought to have found out the facts about this man's character. The Finance Minister bases his whole case on the failure of Mr. Fielding to institute an inquiry into the character of Travers. My hon. friend will remember that when he was making his statement I asked him by what legal

authority Mr. Fielding could have instituted an investigation. Could he summon those parties before him to give evidence? The minister had to admit that no such authority exists in the Bank Act. What then, could Mr. Fielding do? Was he not bound to go by the record? Hon. ministers who are listening to me know that every day they are getting advice from various quarters. We on this side of the House are giving them advice, telling them what to do. We make suggestions to them but what do they do? They go down to their offices and turn up the record when they have to arrive at a decision, and on the record they make a decision, not on statements made to them around the corridors of the House. They are bound to go by the record, that is what the late Finance Minister did and he found the record was explicit indeed. For example, we have the oath of Travers which is a specific and positive statement reading as follows:
On the twenty-third day of October, 1906, there had been actually bona fide subscribed five thousand seven hundred and fifty-seven shares of the capital stock of the Farmers Bank of Canada, and I have had personal knowledge of the applications and the subscriptions and each and all of the said subscriptions is and are on the printed form of application-a copy of which is now produced and marked exhibit ' C ' to this my declaration, and that the said subscription appeared on the stock books of the said hank, and that a sum beyond $250,000 thereof in cash has been actually paid in by the subscribers of the same.
Now shown to me and marked exhibit ' D ' to this my declaration is a list of the subscribers to the capital stock of the said bank correctly setting forth as to each subscription the name of the subscriber, his address, the number of shares subscribed for by him, the amount of such shares and the amount paid in thereon. Each of the said subscriptions is a bona fide subscription to the capital stock of the said bank.
Besides, Mr. Fielding had the statement of his deputy and I wish to point out that it is the duty of the officers of the department to ascertain that the details of the law are complied with and not the duty of the minister. It was drawn to the attention of the House that the late Minister of Finance at that time was busy preparing the Budget Speech for that year that it was difficult for him to find even a few minutes to have an interview with Travers. He depended altogether on hie officers, as the present Finance Minister depends on his officers for details of this kind and his deputy in memorandum *stated that everything was regular and

that the time had arrived when the certificate might be issued. Here is the statement of Mr. Boville the deputy minister:
The undersigned has received an application from the Farmers Bank of Canada for a certificate to commence the business of banking.
The papers are all in order and have been submitted to the Department of Justice, who have advised that the evidence contained therein is such that the Treasury Board may lawfully accept it and issue the necessary certificate.
In connection with the papers it will be noticed that in the list of shareholders the information covers the amount paid by each shareholder on his subscription. This information was supplied at the request of the undersigned as a test of the good faith of the subscribers. The number of subscribers exceeds 500 . and the stock is fairly -well distributed amongst them.
The undersigned sees no objection to the granting of the certificate required by the Bank ACta
(Sgd) T. C. Boville,
Deputy Minister of Finance. Finance Department, Ottawa,
November 30, 1906.
That is a very specific certificate from the Deputy Minister of Finance, and it is a true statement. There is no blame to be placed at the door of the deputy minister. In the face of this affidavit and of the certificate of the deputy minister, how can we say that there was any negligence on the part of the late Minister of Finance?
But the Government decided to appoint a Royal Commission. They selected a very competent man, the chief justice of this province, to conduct the inquiry, and I have no doubt that at the time of that appointment some of them at least expected a different decision from the one they got. It reminds me of the 'Biblical story of Balaam, the son of Beor, wbo was appealed to to curse the people of God, and who, instead of cursing them, blessed them. It was expected that Sir William Meredith would find Mr. Fielding guilty, but instead of that he completely exonerated Mr. Fielding of any negligence in this matter. The question for the House to ascertain is what was the proximate cause of this loss? The chief justice of Ontario in his judgment states positively that it was not the granting of the certificate, but the fraud and negligence of the manager of the bank and his associates. Here is his decision:
Notwithstanding the irregularities on the part of Travers and his misconduct in connection with the application for the certificate, which I have mentioned, the evidence satisfies me that if the bank had been prudently and honestly managed there is no reason why it should not have succeeded. The promissory notes that had been given by subscribers were for the most

part good and were subsequently paid, and while It is true that if the certificate of the Treasury Board had not been granted the money of the shareholders and depositors would not have been lost, the efficient cause of that loss was the recklessness and fraud of those entrusted with the management of the bank, and not the granting of the certificate.
Surely that is specific enough. In the face of that judgment it is idle to say that there was any negligence on the part of the exMinister of Finance. The argument has been used by my hon. friend the Minister of Finance and criticised by various speakers that if the certificate had not been issued there would have been no bank, and there being no bank there would have been no depositors, and there being no depositors there would have been no loss. That is a very fallacious argument, as can easily be seen if we go one step further back and say that if Travers had never been born he would never have been a bank promoter, and if he had never been a bank promoter he would never have come knocking at the door of Parliament for a certificate, and if there had been no certificate there would have been no Farmers Bank and no loss; therefore, the whole blame lies on the father and -mother of Travers; they are the guilty parties.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The Government
had no notice with respect to the matter to which my hon. friend has alluded.

That is no doubt true,
and I do not know what action they could have taken if it had received notice. Possibly some way or other might have been found of meeting the Situation. The plain truth, if we must tell it, is that the Government is proposing to pay the political debts of certain supporters in the province of Ontario. A good deal of discussion took place on the second reading of this Bill as to whether or not the Minister of Labour had promised that if he were elected in 1911 he would support a measure to reimburse the depositors of the Farmers Bank. My hon. friend has admitted that he did make such a statement to the electors of his own constituency. I think I shall be able to show from the Conservative press of Ontario that he promised the same thing outside his own constituency. A few weeks ago I took the trouble of searching the files of the leading papers in that part of Ontario for the month of September, 1911, and I found that the pages of these newspapers are dotted all over with statements of that kind. In various places, meetings were held at that time at which the principal subject under discussion was the payment of the losses in connection with the Farmers Bank. I have been told by people who ought to know that the London Free Press is one of the most orthodox Conservative papers in Ontario-if I am wrong in that some hon. gentleman will correct me. I searched the files of that paper for some two or three weeks prior to the election. I found reports of several meetings that had been held in the constituencies affected and at which promises had been made by candidates. The Kerwood meeting has already been referred to. I find by the London Free Press that there were present on the platform at that meeting Hon. W. J. Hanna, Hon. T. W. Crothers, James Cobban, the Conservative candidate for West Middlesex, and George Elliot, now member for North Middlesex. These gentlemen were leaders of the Conservative party in the province of Ontario. Mr. Waddell, secretary of an organization composed of people who lost money in the Farmers Bank, appeared at the meeting, where the following questions were asked the candidates:
Would the candidate support a measure in the House of Commons to firing financial relief to the depositors in the Farmers Bank who lost by its collapse?
According to the newspaper reports, that pledge was taken by the candidates. The London Free Press devoted three columns to a graphic report of the speech of the Minister of Labour at that meeting under the following flaming head lines:
Conservative party ready to right losses in Farmers Bank due to Fielding's negligence. T. W. Crothers declares at Kerwood that country is responsible for the results that came from neglect of its official agent. Not only the depositors hut the shareholders as well should be recompensed for the financial loss they incurred in the bank crash.
It goes on to say:
Mr. Crothers gave a splendid address, dealing not only with reciprocity but also with the Farmers Bank, the Lanctot case and other matters of concern. He made it plain that the Conservative party if returned to power on the 21st would take steps to see that immediate justice was done to those who lost by the failure of the Farmers Bank, and the compensation would apply not only to the depositors hut to the shareholders as well.
It is only fair to say that the minister qualified that statement the other day on the second reading of the Bill by saying that he spoke for himself and not for the Conservative party, but the London Free Press repeatedly states in its reports that he did speak for the Conservative party.

and I have searched the files of the London Free Press in vain for any repudiation by the Minister of Labour of that statement credited to him under those flaring headlines. So that there should be no doubt about the matter, the Free Press goes on to quote Mr. Crothers' exact words:
I am in favour of indemnifying every man who lost a dollar by the operations of the management of the Farmers Bank. Some people have said that the depositors only should have their losses made good, but I hold that others are in the same position as the depositors. .	.	. We intend to see that every
man who lost will be recouped.
I also find that at the meeting at Fingal on the 4th of September, 1911, the Minister of Labour is reported as having used almost the identical language he used at the Kerwood meeting. He says:
I am in favour of indemnifying every man who lost a dollar by the operations of the management of the Farmers Bank. Some people have said that only the losses of the depositors should be made good, but I hold that others are in the same position as the depositors. .	. We intend to see that every man
who lost shall be reimbursed.
Who are 'we'?

That is the question. Does the use of the word ' we ' mean that the hon. gentleman spoke for himself or the party to which he belongs?
Then, on another page of this newspaper, I found a reference to the election which was being held in South Huron and I will give you this extract. This extract is taken from the Free Press of the 15th of September, 1911:
In South Huron the Farmers Bank is the chief issue and Mr. M. T. McLean the member, will lose a good many supporters owing to his stand on this issue, and this riding is looked upon as a Conservative gain on September 21.
The prophecy which the Free Press made on, the 15th of September, 1911, that my good old friend1, Mr. M. Y. McLean, would be defeated on account of the Farmers Bank situation, came true, I am sorry to say. As you know, Mr. Speaker, Mr. McLean was not returned on that occasion, and I think we can safely say that this was the issue on which a number of seats were carried in the province of Ontario and that a number of hon. gentlemen hold their seats to-day in this House owing to the fact that they promised to pay the losses of the Farmers Bank at the time when they were running their elections.

As representing South
Huron I may speak for myself.
Order.
I am referring to what was stated in this newspaper.
May I ask the hon. gentleman a question?
I was pointing out that what was stated in the newspaper proved to be true.

The Farmers Bank was
not an issue on my part. On the other side Mr. McLean used it as an issue. He got up before the people and admitted that he had voted against the resolution to appoint a commission.

He was honest in so
doing, and that is the reason, I suppose, of his defeat.

But he promised that
he would do all he could to see that the depositors were reimbursed.

There is no proof of
that statement. I wish to put a question to you, Mr. Speaker. You are one of the oldest members of this House, you have had a greater experience in political matters than perhaps any other member within hearing of my voice. You know the election law and the proper conduct of a candidate running an election perhaps better than any other man in Canada; I wish to a3k you what would you think of a cash offer of this kind being made by any hon. gentleman on the occasion of an election. I will assume if you like that there was a claim against the Government although to my mind it makes no difference whether there was a claim or not. Is it a proper thing for an hon. gentleman under such circumstances to get up on a platform at the time of an election when he is a candidate asking for the votes of the pepple and say to them:	If you vote for me, or
for my party, I will vote for a measure that will put money into your pockets. Suppose a candidate had outstanding personal obligations. It is unfortunately true that members of Parliament like other people are sometimes in debt. Suppose a candidate under such circumstances got on the platform in the presence of a lot of electors to whom he owed money and said: If you vote for me, and if I am elected, I will pay the debt. If a candidate did that, he would be disqualified; and yet we have

a minister of the Crown getting up in his place in this House and admitting that he did make such a promise on a public platform to the electors of his constituency, and he said that he was not ashamed of doing it. I submit he should be ashamed.
I ask you, Mr. Speaker, what you think of a case of that kind and if you think a man is justified, even if he believes there i.s a proper claim against the Government for the payment of these losses, in standing on a public platform and making a cash offer to the people whose votes he is soliciting.

I would ask the
hon. gentleman his authority for that statement and whether, he has any one in particular in mind when he makes it. I do not ask this question with a view to embarrassing the hon. gentleman but for information and in view of the peculiar statement that was made here by a candidate already nominated who, while speaking on the second reading of this Bill the other night, said: I shall be forced, I am afraid, to vote for this Bill?

I have in my mind
several hon. members. There were some hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House who repudiated the fact that they had made such a promise. There were other gentlemen who did not say whether they had made the promise or not and there was one hon. gentleman at least who boldly admitted that he had made it, and rather boasted of it.	I wish to
submit that I think it was very improper that such a promise should be made on the occasion of an election by any person, and especially by a candidate. It reminds me of a story that is told about a candidate in Nova Scotia. He was making a personal canvass, going from house to house and asking electors if they would vote for him. He appealed to a man who had a vote, and undertook to argue the ease with him. He said: I am supporting the National Policy. The man took no interest in that argument. He then talked to him about the record of the party, but that did not seem to interest him either. He then said something about the old flag, but the man was still indifferent. Then he talked about the iniquity of truck and trade with the Yankees, but could make no impression at all upon the voter. Finally he took him around the corner of the barn and gave him $5. At once the man's eye kindled and he said: ' Mister, them's the arguments.' I submit,
Mr. Speaker, it was the same arguments that were used by hon. gentlemen opposite when they appealed to the electors of On-tari on the ground that they would support a measure to pay this $1,200,000 to the people who had lost their money through this unfortunate failure.
Is that a fair average of the Liberals of Nova Scotia?

I think that from what, my hon. friend (Mr. Wright) has heard me say he will understand that it is a long time since the Liberals in Nova Scotia have been canvassing people on the National Policy or in opposition to truck and trade with the Yankees. He can draw his own inference about that.	.
A good deal has been said in this discussion about the iniquity of taking promissory notes for subscriptions. I never knew that it was a crime to sign a promissory note in settlement of a debt or to subscribe for stock. Sir William Meredith does not say that there was anything illegal in the making of the promissory notes. It has been said that if Mr. Fielding had known that the promissory notes were given for subscriptions, and if he had known that these promissory notes were discounted without recourse he would have been justified in refusing the certificate. I do not think he would have been. It is somewhat irregular, but the object of the law is to see that a certain amount of capital is paid up, and when that capital is as a matter of fact paid up the spirit of the law is complied with. When Mr. Travers obtained these notes from the subscribers, took them to the trust company, endorsed them to the trust company and got the cash without recourse, and when the trust company	held the makers of
the notes for their debts, I think we can say	that Travers had the
money just as completely as if the money had been taken by each individual subscriber out of his till and paid into his hand. A sample form of the notes used in - this case is given on page 727 of the exhibits, as follows:
Toronto, June 27, 1906.

Twelve months after date I promise to pay to the order of the provisional directors of the Farmers Bank of Canada fourty five hundred dollars at the office of the Farmers Bank of Canada, Toronto, for value received.
This is signed by the subscriber and endorsed a3 follows:

Pay to the order of W. R. Travers, John Ferguson, Alex Fraser, Jas. Gallighar, A. L. Lown, John Watson, without recourse, per W. R. Travers, attorney.
(Sgd) W. R. Travers.
These notes were then turned over to the trust company and endorsed 'without recourse.' Consequently the money was in the hands of the bank directors in such a way that it could not be taken back from them. Even if those subscribers failed to pay their notes at maturity, the trust company would have no recourse on Travers or his associates to get the money back. I would consider the case very different if the notes had the usual endorsement, and if, after the six or twelve months had expired, the subscribers made default. In that case the trust company could come to Mr. Travers and call for the money, and in order to meet this call he might be compelled to take the money out of the funds of the bank. As the notes, however, are endorsed 'without recourse,' this could not happen, and I believe that is the reason why the commissioner did not find much fault with the fact that the notes were given. My hon. friend the Prime Minister drew attention to the fact that the commissioner said a breach of trust had been committed. I understand the breach of trust referred to by the commissioner was that the directors abrogated their functions; turned over the whole business to Mr. Travers, and allowed him to do just as he pleased with the notes. These directors were the trustees of the shareholders, and it was their duty to carry out the trust and not to hand that duty over to any one. There is no fraud in connection with the making of the notes at all. The fraud is in the way that the notes were handled afterwards, and in the wording of the affidavit made by Mr. Travers in which he swore that cash had been paid when, as a matter of fact, the cash was not paid at first but afterwards when he negotiated the notes and got the cash without recourse from the trust company.
We on this side of the House claim that, if there is to be legislation, it should apply not only to the Farmers Bank but to all similar cases. I have no hesitation in saying that the principle of this Bill is bad. The taxpayers of Canada should not be responsible for mistakes of this kind, if indeed there is any mistake. At the same time, under the disclosures that have been made in this debate and the facts that have been brought to the attention of the Government relating to the way

banking institutions are being financed, it might be well that a thorough investigation should take place. I have drawn attention to the fact of the situation in Prince Edward Island. My hon. friend from Kouville (Mr. Lemieux) has drawn attention to the fact that there was gross negligence on the part of the Department of Finance prior to 1896 in the case of La Banque Ville Marie. I am opposed to the legislation; but I do not think there can be any good objection to a thorough investigation.
My hon. friend from North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) said that the Farmers Bank was conceived in iniquity. That is my idea of this Bill. It belongs to the same breed as the bank; it is a vicious proposal, and should not receive the assent of this House. I think every business man within my hearing knows that it is questionable whether a single bank can be named, that has been started in Canada within the last twenty-five years, that has been altogether free from the same irregularity. I am able to make the statement that some of the leading banks in Canada, when they issue new stock, are quite ready to accept the notes of old subscribers for the new stock. They turn these notes into their books and call it cash and issue circulation on it. Whether this is irregular or not, it has been the practice in the old and well-established banking institutions and I do not assume to condemn it. There is nothing criminal about making a note of hand providing a man meets the same when due. If that was a criminal act a good many of us would be in the penitentiary. In view of all these facts and the disclosures that have been made, I beg to move the following resolution, seconded by Mr. Demers:
That this Bill be not now read a third time, hut be referred back to the Committee of the Whole House for the purpose of adding the following clause:
This Act shall not come into force until after an investigation by a Royal Commission into all losses incurred by depositors by reason of failures of Canadian chartered banks since July 1, 1867.

Mr. Speaker, in accordance with what I understand to be your ruling I should like to put myself on record in a few words upon this question. I should like to do so in accordance with what I understand to be not a rule, which is nevertheless a tradition of Parliament, that the remarks on the third reading of a Bill should be reasonably brief.

I do not know whether to approach the merits of this question seriously. I do not know whether the Government mean the proposition seriously; that is to say, as a proposition in statesmanship. I am quite sure they mean it seriously as a proposition in electioneering. We would scarcely consider a session of Parliament normal under this Government if, towards the close, we did not have something in the nature of what I venture to call political vagrancy on the part of the province of Ontario. The first session of this Parliament saw a proposition to give $2,000,000 to a railroad that was a perfectly profitable and going concern in northern Ontario at the expense of the rest of the taxpayers of this country. That proposition was renewed last Parliament; and unfortunately .the Senate weakened in its opposition and the proposition became law, although it was a most unnecessary piece of legislation. But that piece of legislation pales in its unnecessary and unjustifiable character in the presence of this proposition.
I would like, in the closing days and, I hope, the closing hours of this session, to impress upon my hon. friend the Minister of Finance once more the seriousness of the position he holds in this country. Just consider the condition of the country today in which this proposition is brought before us. I was horrified, as a good Canadian, to read last night that in the last ten days of May, the decrease in the takings of that great undertaking, the Canadian Pacific railway, was $806,000, which is at the rate of $2,400,000 of a decrease in the takings of that great railroad in one month. That is an indication, a perfect indication, of the present condition of this country; and it is under these conditions that my hon. friend -brings forth a proposition to give away $1,200,000 of this country 's money to recoup the depositors in -a bank that failed. I venture to say, Sir, that no such outrageous, no such monstrous proposition, was ever brought before the deliberative assembly of a civilized country. I say that advisedly; if I were called upon to describe this proposition in language, I should havf to go far beyond1 the adjectives I have just used, and would inevitably bring myself under your ruling. This proposition-the iniquity of it-appeals peculiarly to western men, and I speak in the presence of my hon. friend the hon. Minister of Public Works (Mr. Rogers), who is a western man, and a good representative of the West. I wish he would tell the House now, in a
few straight words-and he never makes long speeches-what, in his heart of hearts, he thinks about this proposition. He has ability to conceal his thoughts, even when he speaks, that is, as great as that of anyone in the ranks of statesmen; but if he were to use a few straight words and tell us what he really thinks of this proposition, it would be a revelation, I am' sure, even to the Minister of Finance. This measure is for the relief of the electors of one section of one province, at the expense of the electors of the other eight provinces, and I appeal to the Minister of Public Works, in these last moments of the session, to re-think this question and bring his views to bear, and the real views of western Canada, upon the Minister of Finance to withdraw this legislation. Do not go through the farce of sending it to the Senate.
What is the merit of this proposition in the opinion of hon. gentlemen opposite? What is it meant for? What was the promise meant for? It was to get votes; there is no possibility of denying that. Well, what ds the proposed redemption of that promise for? It is a political proposition of the most iniquitous kind, a political proposition pure and simple. We had the principle upon which this measure was based, as it is regarded in the province of Ontario, laid down by my hon. friend from East Simcoe (Mr. Bennett). When a previous proposition was before the House to give -millions to a railway company, that hon. gentleman said, in answer to a suggestion of mine:	Of course this Government owes a great deal to Ontario, look at the supporters they get from Ontario. This does not appeal to western Canada, and I would impress this view upon the Minister of Public Works and equally upon the Solicitor General (Mr. Meighen). Voltaire, in one of his most cynical moments, said that it is the main duty of governments to take money from one section of the community and give it to another. Well, what that great cynic said at the end of the eighteenth century, was not only a piece of cynicism but a very accurate prophecy of the moral actions of this Government. It is their principal form of ability-to take money from one section of the community and give it to another. I appeal to my hon. friends from the West to join with me in resisting this raid upon the electors of British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, and Manitoba; and equally I appeal to the representatives of Quebec and the Maritime provinces to resist

this raid upon them for the benefit of the supporters of the party that happens to find itself in power, for the vote of one particular province, the province of Ontario.
On the merits of this question before the House-or rather on its demerits, for as I have said its merits do not exist for western Canada-surely nothing less than temerity actuates the ministers from Ontario and their supporters, to come to the West and ask for the support of this proposition. Sir, at the very time when these promises were being made to Ontario, what was Ontario doing, and what have her representatives been doing since for the people of the West, which has to contribute a large share of this money for the depositors of the bank? They were refusing us the opportunity of making the money. The Minister of Finance has been compared to various Scriptural and other characters of a more or less questionable nature, but his attitude on this subject reminds me of Pharoah at one period of his career. The hon. gentlemen will remember that at one time Pharoah gave [DOT] .the poor Israelitish helots, straw to make the bricks that he demanded of them. But he grew worse as he went along, and the time came when he said to the children of Israel: Gather your straw where you can, but do not fail to bring your whole tale of bricks. So the Minister of Finance and his supporters say to the people of the West: You shall not make money, but what little money you do make we must have the whole tale of it for the people who voted us into power in Ontario.
On the merits of the question: Does the Minister of Finance intend to repair all the mistakes of previous Administrations in this country, or even the mistakes of the Administration that preceded his own in power? Does he take upon his shoulders duties of that arduous nature-and he so very young? I pity him if he is going along these lines to. discover and to right the errors even of the previous Government. I am not going to admit the errors. I have not, as I have indicated from time to time, too much confidence in my hon. friend's finance, and it appears to me that there are grounds, furnished in the very excellent speech of my hon. friend from Kingston (Mr. Nickle) why we should not have too much confidence in his law. I rather think the hon. member for Kingston had the better of him in that bout on a question of law. I am going to continue to get the better of him in finance and economic science in argument anyhow. If he is beaten in the realm of law by the hon. member for Kingston, and in the

realm of finance and economics by others, I do not know where his versatile genius is going to lead him to get off at. Does he really set out to repair the errors of previous Administrations? The principle is utterly vicious; the Administration is dead; its acts are dead-that seems to be the common sense of it. These men made an unfortunate investment, as the result of the Act of the previous Administration, and they should stand by the result. I wonder at the citizens of Ontario allowing their minister to bring this proposition before Parliament. If there is one thing more than another that in my twelve and a-half years' residence in Canada I have learned to admire in the average Canadian, it is that he takes the kicks and cuffs of adverse fortune without unmanly squealing. When the average Canadian gets down in business, I notice he soon tries to get up. I wonder that they allow a proposition to be brought before Parliament that they should have the results of their own indiscretion-to say the least of it-made up to them as a gift from the rest of the nation. That is a fine proposition. It is a premium upon indiscretion on the part of the depositors. What is it that causes people to put their money into faulty concerns? It is the prospect of large interest. We have had it stated here very confidently this afternoon, that one per cent extra interest was offered these depositors. I see my hon. friend from Bruce (Mr. Hugh Clark) shaking his head. I say the statement has been made here very confidently, and not successfully contradicted, that extra interest was promised these men. From the moral standpoint, in going into this thing at all they were actuated by greed, and the Government comes forward to reward them for having gambled for one per cent extra interest by making up to them the loss of the original deposits. That is from the moral standpoint; from the intellectual standpoint where is the defence of these men in coming to Parliament? Where is the defence of the Government in coming before Parliament for them with a proposition of this kind? Morally they were actuated by greed; intellectually they were actuated by indiscretion, and this proposal is a premium upon indiscretion added to greed. On the part of conductors of banks, it is an encouragement of fraud. I submit that not only by the fear of punishment are the managers of institutions like this deterred from wrongdoing. A great deterring in-

fluence in such cases is the knowledge, which exists in that part of all men that is good, that if they do wrong they will hurt others. I submit that statesmen and legislators should take cognizance of the force of that statement: that a wise deterrent is put in us and in men of prominence by Providence that if they do wrong in positions of trust they will hurt other people. But if the Government come along and say: look at these poor widows and orphans, we must relieve them; if the Government take this attitude, they take away that deterring inAuence and they encourage fraud on the part of the conductors of such institutions.
This proposal is not only a premium on indiscretion and greed on the part of depositors and an encouragement to fraud on the part of those conducting the institution, but it provides an absolutely vicious precedent, and that is, of course, by far the most serious aspect of the case from the point of view of the interests of the nation. It establishes a precedent. Does my hon. friend think that a change of government at the next election is an impossibility? It is not an impossibility; it is a very great probability if the Canadian PaciAc railway receipts go down to the tune of $2,500,000 a month much longer, as they are doing at the present moment. It is a very great probability; and let me say to my hon. friend the member for South Victoria (Mr. Barnard) that if the conditions in British Columbia get much worse than they are at the present moment, a change of government is quite probable. I notice that my hon. friend smiles; he is always good-natured, and I am glad to make some answer to his smile. I had a letter the other day from one of the oldest residents of the province- he has been there thirty-one years-and he says that any period of previous depression in British Columbia is skinned by miles by this one. He says that he understands that the Government are waiting on Providence to trim the Senate, but that Providence is ' sure ' trimming them. It is not an impossibility that the Government may go out at the next election, and I put it to my hon. friend, in the event of their going out, what does he expect will be the result of this legislation if it passes into law? I put the question to my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I would like him to make a speech in defence of something that is brought forward by my hon. friend the Minister of Finance, but I value his reputation so much that I would not like to see him make a speech in defence of this legislation. It would test even his dialectic ability to put this thing forward in a good light, and I would advise him to follow the rule which he and I have followed to a considerable extent this year, that of maintaining a discreet silence in the House except on odd occasions. What does he think will be the effect of this legislation supposing there is a change of government? Do you think that the people of other provinces, let us say the province of Quebec, who are probably not wholly unamenable to political debauchery; does he think that they will not beneAt by the experience of the people of the province of Ontario? Has my hon. friend not heard in the course of the present debate questions asked and points raised about banks that have failed in Quebec? Is the Government prepared to open out a long future vista of proceedings of this nefarious character? If they are, then I for one want to tell them that they are doing something which is nothing short of holding out a temptation to politicians to go before the electors with debauching propositions that actual money will be made up to men who have lost, provided they return a certain party to .power, il put it to the Government, could anything be more deleterious to the public life, could anything be more degrading to public men; could anything be more demoralizing to the electorate of Canada?
This legislation establishes a vicious precedent, and it is opposed to the wishes of the majority of the people of this country. I do not think that a member of the Government having a sense of responsibility would dare to rise in his place and say that he would wish to see this question, from the point of view of party success, submitted to the electors from Halifax to Vancouver upon its merits. <1 say that, except from the most violent partisans, it would not get a vote outside of the province of Ontario, and I think sufficiently of the political integrity of Ontario to believe that such a proposition would be voted down in that province as well. On these grounds: that it is a premium on indiscretion and greed; that it is an encouragement of fraud; that it establishes a vicious precedent, the end of which we cannot possibly see; that it is opposed to the wishes of the great majority of the people of this country, I venture, on my personal responsibility, to express the hoipe that the Senate, as at present constituted, will add

to the number of grounds which it has for the gratitude of this countiy by saving the nation from what is nothing less than an act of political burglary.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. T. WHITE (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not propose to debate further the principle involved in this measure. I agree with the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat (Mr. Michael Clark) that the discussion upon third reading ought to be a3 brief as possible. I have heard my hon. friend the member for Red Deer upon many occasions in this House on which matters of moment and importance were under consideration. I have seen him keep his seat when large expenditures were being voted for the public purposes; I have seen him undisturbed by votes involving large donations to railway companies by way of subsidies. His voice has been silent upon more than one occasion when guarantees to such companies were under consideration by the House: I have never heard him rise to such a height of indignation as he did this afternoon, when the question before the House is whether this country, to use the words of his right hon. leader, is big enough to do simple justice to the depositors of this bank, which, on the evidence before the House, should not have been allowed to open its doors for business. I think that my hon. friend's eloquence might be much better employed than against the just claims of these people, many of whom have been reduced to the most abject poverty by the depredations of this bank throughout the province of Ontario.
My hon. friend refers to the grant made last year to the Ontario Government in respect of the Temiskaming and Northern Ontario Railway Company as a political outrage. I have never heard my hon friend protest against any grant by way of subsidy to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, or to the Canadian Northern Railway Company. If Mackenzie and Mann had built the Temiskaming and Northern Ontario railway and had opened up a rich district to the north, no question would have arisen; they would have received a subsidy. But when the province of Ontario has had the courage to embark upon an enterprise which has opened up one of the richest districts in Canada, the voice of my hon. friend is heard in indignant protest. Millions for the Grand Trunk Pacific railway, millions foT the Canadian Northern railway by way of subsidy, but not one dollar for the province

of Ontario with respect to its public enterprise.
The other is a federal undertaking.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I must say I fail to follow the argument of my hon. friend. It is well known that subsidies have been justified in the past by all governments to railway companies which open up a virgin territory, and if ever there was a case of a pioneer road opening up such a territory, a road whose construction has been justified by the result, it was the Temiskaming and Northern Ontario railway. I say that the province of Ontario did not come here as a suppliant in this matter, they came as a matter of right. They said in substance: You are giving subsidies to the Canadian Northern railway, you are giving subsidies to the Canadian Pacific railway; all that we ask is that you put us on the same basis as private enterprise and give a subsidy to this road which is government-owned. I find very little sympathy on the part of hon. gentlemen opposite in connection with public ownership. Now my hon. friend has asked me if I am going to take all the mistakes of the late Administration on my shoulders. In answer I say I am no Atlas and do not pretend to pose as one. I shall take their mistakes neither on my back nor on my conscience-and the latter would be as heavy a load as the former. Now we come to the amendment of my hon. friend from Guysborough, and I think the House will agree that it is a most extraordinary amendment indeed. He provides in it that this Act shall not come into force until after an investigation by a royal commission into all losses incurred by depositors by reason of failures of Canadian chartered banks since July 1, 1867. That would be a very large order. I have before me here a list of twenty-four banks that have failed or gone into liquidation since 1867. The amendment of my hon. friend involves an investigation into all the affairs of these banks. I observe that some of them were incorporated as long ago as between 1830 and 1840, so that the investigation which this amendment has in view would involve some twenty-four banks and would extend in time over a period of about eighty years. I think that if that were undertaken by the Government this Bill would come into force about the date of the battle of Armageddon and, as the hon. Solicitor General pointed out, the legislation in this case of the Farmers Bank is not to depend

in any way upon the result. Let me put this to my hon. friend. Supposing that an individual has a just claim of a certain kind against the Dominion. What would he think of the Dominion taking this position: We will not pay this claim until we have held an inquiry, summoning before us every other citizen of Canada, to see if he has a similar claim and what the merits of it are. That is about as logical as this amendment.
Oh, no.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Let me put it in this way. Supposing this is a just claim, and the Government says it is a claim which we are morally bound to meet.
A political claim.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend may say a political claim, but we do not say so. Supposing this is a claim which the Government feels it is incumbent on it to pay.

My hon. friend can get over that difficulty by making the>
Act general, providing for payment of all just claims.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Is there any reason why we should cause these depositors to wait for the reinbursement to which they are entitled on the ground of equity and justice, until we have held an investigation into all banks that have failed in the Dominion of Canada since 1867 ? I think my hon. friend will see that the amendment involves an absurdity and cannot by any possibility be justified. I would submit that in the case of any application being made to the Government for relief such as this, a prima facie case must be established on the part of those putting forward the claim. A prima facie case was made out in the case of the Farmers Bank before a commission of inquiry was instituted. Verbal and written evidence had been laid before the House, an exhaustive debate had been held on the subject and a very strong prima facie case made out. Then a commission was appointed to investigate the affairs of the bank as to its organization, as to the issue of the certificate, and as to the subsequent conduct of its affairs. That report has been before us and has been under discussion.
Does not the minister pay any attention to what is said by Mr. Justice Meredith, that the failure was not due to the fault of Mr. Fielding, but to the fault of the board of directors ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend has been absent from the House. That contention was put forward and disposed of without any difficulty.
Not at all, only in the mind of the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Sir William Meredith made a most specific finding that it was the duty of the Treasury Board to have made an inquiry.
And did not the chief justice find that Mr. Fielding was not in fault but that the failure was due entirely to the mismanagement of the manager of the bank.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, he found it was incumbent on the Treasury Board to have made a certain investigation which they failed to make. If that investigation had been made the certificate would not have been issued.	.	[DOT]
Notwithstanding that fact, the failure was due to mismanagement and not to Mr. Fielding.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am dealing with the finding of the commission, and if my hon. friend reads it he will find that, in the opinion of the commissioner, it was the duty of the Treasury Board to make an investigation which they failed to make. If they had made that investigation they would have discovered the character of Travers, they would have discovered the irregularities complained of, and this bank would never have been started on its ill-fated career.
It would have stopped Travers investing in the Keely mine?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Travers would not have been manager. They would have discovered his character in the investigation which the Chief Justice says it was incumbent on the Treasury Board to have made. My hon. friend cannot get away from that.
Why did not the directors who engaged Travers make the investigation ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Why didn't they? I am sure I cannot tell. The fact is that they did not.
That was not the business of Mr. Fielding.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have heard all kinds of arguments put forward here to show the alleged absurdity of the contention that if



this bank had not been started there would not have been any loss. I heard it stated in this House that you might as well have said that if the Empress of Ireland had not been constructed the loss of life would not have taken place in the recent catastrophe. But let me put this forward: Supposing that, as a matter of fact, it was the statutory duty of this Government to see that no ship was built, let us say unless with horizontal bulkheads instead of transverse bulkheads. Let us assume that the Government did permit a ship to be built in that way and that a catastrophe had been brought about by reason of the ship being so built. I am not at all certain that there would not be a moral claim on the Government in connection with a dereliction of duty in the superintending of the building of that ship.
But supposing that the disaster did not result from that but from some other cause?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
What did these Farmers
Bank losses result from? They resulted from the fraud, dishonesty and mismanagement of Travers. If the Treasury Board had made the investigation which the commissioner finds it was incumbent upon them to have made, the bank with Travers at its head would never have opened its doors for business. There is a clear connection between the failure of the Treasury Board to have made that investigation and the lossess which subsequently resulted to the unfortunate depositors.
Suppose this supposititious ship with the bulkheads not properly built, becomes a wreck. What happens then?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It would depend upon all the facts of the case. We have had the facts in this case investigated and the commissioner finds that the Treasury Board was negligent. There is no doubt about that.
There was no negligence.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Let me ask a question of my hon. friend, who is a good lawyer. If it is incumbent upon a board to make a certain inquiry and they fail to make that inquiry is not that negligence?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The chief justice found that it was an error of judgment.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Does my right hon. friend mean to say that an error of judgment is not negligence? My right hon. friend knows

that every man is held to exercise the judgment which the average man should exercise, and that if he fails'to exercise that judgment he is negligent. The depositors and their committees urged on the different candidates all through Ontario the making of that promise.
