I deny that assertion; I did say at that time that if I were elected I would do what I could to bring relief to the depositors of the Farmers Bank.

I do not know that there is much difference between the statement which I made and the statement made by my hon. friend. However, I did not promise absolutely to vote for any measure that would be brought forward for the reimbursement of the Farmers Bank depositors, and what I am saying now is amply borne out by my remarks as they appear in ' Hansard ' of 1912-13. On more occasions than one at public meetings I was asked: Will you vote to reimburse the depositors of the Farmers Bank ? I said: I will not make any promise that I will vote for any proposal to reimburse the depositors of the Farmers Bank; I do not think that it is fair for you to ask a public man to make a definite promise to support a proposal before he knows what that proposal will be. I said: My sympathies are all with you; I feel that great suffering has been caused by the failure of this bank. If when I know the facts more fully, a measure is introduced which I think is fair and which my judgment approves, I will use my discretion as your representative as to whether or not I shall support it, and

if you do not want to vote for me on that basis, vote for the other man. I can bring a host of witnesses to corroborate what I say in that regard.
Does the hon. member for West Middlesex deny having written that letter ?
My hon. friend has sought to lead the House to believe that he has in his possession a letter written by me, but it turns out that he has only a copy; I do not know whether it is a copy or not.
Oh, oh.
My hon. friend said that he had a letter written by the hon. member for West Middlesex; has he that letter ?
If the hon. member had been in the House when the debate was resumed, he would have heard me explain that I did have the original, that I had read the original letter, of which this is an exact copy.

The hon. member did not give the original letter. At any rate, I do not care, for there is nothing in the letter which I am ashamed of; the letter bears out exactly what I say. I said to Mr. Waddell: My sympathies are with the depositors of the Farmers Bank, and if any reasonable measure for relief is submitted and has my approval, I shall be glad to support it.

Then my hon. friend
admits that he wrote the letter?

If my hon. friend will show me the original, I will admit it. But, as I say, I am ashamed of nothing in that letter. My hon. friend is rather secretive about the matter; if he has the original, let him send it across the floor of the House. In 1913 they wanted me to promise absolutely, if I were returned to Parliament, to support a measure for the reimbursement of the depositors of the Farmers Bank, but I said: no, I will not; I will reserve my judgment. If I think the proposal put before Parliament is reasonable; if it appeals to my judgment as being fair and right, that will be another matter. I said: I am going to retain the power, if you elect me, to do what I think is right and just, as I think any representative in the House of Commons should do. Let me read what I said in 1913:
The depositors and their committees urged on the different candidates ail through Ontario the making of that promise. For my own part,

I thought it was an unfair advantage to take of any man, and I refused to make that promise. I told my people that X would come back to this House, and if a Bill was introduced that I thought was fair I would support it; if it was not fair in my opinion I would oppose it, and that X would do the best I honestly could for them.
That is as far as I would go and as far as I did go, either publicly or privately, and the letter which the hon. member for North Middlesex read bears out my statement exactly. My hon. friend said that he was at a meeting in Kerwood and that the hon. Minister of Labour did not make a promise of reimbursement. I would refer my hon. friend to the report of his own organ in that regard. It was told by more than one man that promises were made not only that the depositors would be reimbursed, but that the shareholders would be reimbursed also, and that the hon. Minister of Labour went so far as to say: I am sorry for you people, and I think that you ought to get interest both on your deposits and on the money that you lost as shareholders from the day the bank went into liquidation up to the present time. A brother of the gentleman from whom my hon. friend got this letter, Mr. Waddell, asked the minister at that time, as I am informed:	Will you give
your promissory note for it? Of course the hon. Minister of Labour did not give his promissory note.
I am not supporting relief to the depositors of the Farmers Bank because I think that Mr. Fielding was to blame. I do not think that Mr. Fielding was to blame at all. I think that the finding of the commissioner absolutely vindicates the Finance Minister of that day. He said that it was not the issuing of the certificate that caused the losses to the depositors of the Farmers Bank, but the recklessness and hishonesty of Mr. Travers. That was clearly pointed out by the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Nickle) the other night, quite to the discomfiture of the hon. Minister of Finance. I support this measure to afford relief to the depositors of the Farmers Bank on the ground of common humanity. If an accident happened to 6,000 people in the province of Ontario by fire or flood or famine, this Parliament would rush to their assistance without delay. For my own part, I do not care how distress befalls my people, whether it be by failure of a bank, or fire, flood or famine, I am always prepared to givb them relief which is generous and just, and I think that this is a case where the relief is both generous and just.

I do not support this legislation for the reasons given by the Government, for I do not think that there is a shred of reasonableness in some of the arguments which they have made,	but I support it
on	ordinary	humanitarian grounds.
I think this country is large enough and the banks have privileges enough that they should be compelled to give an absolute guarantee to depositors who place money in their hands in trust. We all know that the depositor gets about two and a half per cent interest on his money. The banks enjoy privileges which are not enjoyed by banks in any other country in the world, and they pay not one cent for these privileges. I say that these banks could not carry on business were it not for the great deposits they receive from the thrift, industry and care of the farmers and artisans of this country and this Government, the Government that preceded them, any Government that may follow, is in duty bound to make some provision so that the bank and the Bankers' Association of this country shall absolutely protect the depositors in chartered banks from loss. For these two reasons, on the ground of common humanity and on the ground that I believe as a matter of banking principle that depositors should be protected, I voted for the relief of these depositors, and I think that the people of my county will justify me in that vote.

speakeroldname: Hon. T. W. CROTHERS (Minister of Labour):
speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member for Guysborough, addressing the House this afternoon, more than once took my name in vain, I desire to say a word or two before this motion is put to the House and, referring particularly to this matter, I want to call the attention of the House to the marked distinction between the records of hon. gentlemen sitting on the other side of the House and those sitting on this side. We have an idea that a public pledge should be as sacredly carried out as a private one. We on this side of the House are of opinion that a public man has no more right to betray public confidence than a private individual has to trifle with private trusts. Gentlemen on the other side of the House sat in the cold shades of Opposition for eighteen years and during that time they made promises, publio promises to the people of the country. They were returned to power in 1896 and they continued in power for fifteen years; and during the whole of that time they never attempted to carry out but one of the
many promises they had made while in Opposition. When in Opposition they told us, the present leader of the Opposition declared to the people of this country, that if he were returned to power he would reduce the public expenditure by $3,000,000 or $4,000,000 a year. He came into power in 1896 and immediately proceeded to double the expenditure of the country. He told the people that if placed in power he would hold the public land for the actual settler. He came into power and distributed it by hundreds of thousands of acres-
Order.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think the hon member is mapping out a route which is wandering away from the third reading of the Bill. I would therefore ask him to keep t< the subject.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: We have been accused of making promises. I wanted to show that we made this promise when in Opposition.
On the Farmers Bank?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: Just keep still. Yes, touching the Farmers Bank; and I wanted to point out the distinction between the course taken by the party on this side of the House when they came into power in 1911 and the course taken by hon. gentle-,men opposite when they came into power in 1896.
Did the hon. minister promise, in Kerwood, to reimburse the shareholders?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think I very fully answered that question the day before yesterday. I do not mind answering it now. I said the day before yesterday, and I want to say now, that our view was that pledges made while we were in Opposition ought to be carried out when we came into power, and we proceeded at the very first session of the House after we came into power to implement the promises we made when in Opposition. One of the promises we made when in Opposition, in substance, was that we would appoint a commission to inquire into the affairs of the Farmers Bank, and, if the report upon that inquiry justified us in so acting, we would do something for the depositors of tihe Farmers Bank. So that we are just now carrying out the promise we made when in Opposition. I then expressed the conviction that Parliament should do something to relieve the depositors of the Farmers Bank. Since I became

a member of this House my custom was, before I became too busy as a minister, to go through my constituency after every session and call the attention of the electors to the material points of what had been said and done during the session. After the dissolution of the House in 1911 I took the same course, and, among other things, I called their attention to what had been done in this House respecting the Farmers Bank. I always spoke for myself; I mentioned no other gentleman's name or his views or expressions in this House. I pointed out to my constituents that in March, 1911, when there was no election in sight, I declared that my conviction was that Parliament should do something to relieve the depositors from the losses they had sustained in moneys misappropriated and squandered by the manager of that bank. In speaking to my constituents in that town I repeated these words, and do not wish to take back a word I uttered, nor am I ashamed of a word I uttered, as the hon. member for Guysborough would try to lead this House to believe. I pointed out to them what I said when there was no election in view. I said I had not changed my views, and, if re-elected, I would do all in my power to see that their losses were recouped. :I made that statement on my own behalf, mentioning nobody else, not assuming to speak for the party. I did not profit any by it; I was simply doing what I had done after every session since I became a member of this House. What are the facts? You will pardon a personal reference. In 1906 I was elected by a majority of 518. In 1911 I was elected by a majority of 987, and the only polling subdivision in my constituency where my majority fell off was the polling subdivision where there was a branch of the Farmers Bank. Let me tell you how that came about. My opponent, amongst others, came to Ottawa a short time before the election on behalf of those interested in the Farmers Bank in that constituency. He met with others here. He saw the Finance Minister, Mr. Fielding. I do not know what the Finance Minister told him, and I do not know personally what he told the electors when he went back; but I was informed, and the result of the polls there convinced me that there was truth in it, that he told a number of my supporters generally that he had been down to Ottawa, that he had seen the Finance Minister, and that the Finance Minister had told him that if the Laurier Govern-
ment were sustained at the polls they would reimburse the depositors of the Farmers Bank. I do not want any one to go away with the idea that I am stating that as being the truth, because, personally, I do not know it, but I heard it. I do state as a fact that there was some influence at work in that particular polling subdivision, because it was the only one in the riding where my majority was reduced.
Several hon. gentlemen opposite have given us hypothetical cases alleged to be analogous to this one. For instance, my hon. friend from Guyeiborough (Mr. iSin-clair) said: Suppose the Minister of Marine and Fisheries were to appoint a man, who had been highly recommended to him as a pilot on the St, Lawrence. The (pilot takes the ship which collides with another vessel, as happened to the Empress of Ireland the other day, and sinks. Would this Government, he asked, think of reimbursing the owners of that vessel? I submit that the cases are not analogous at all. Let me give an analogous case. Suppose a man applied to the Minister of Marine for a position as pilot, and that four or five reputable men were to tell the minister before he made the appointment that the applicant was a man who used intoxicating liquors to excess, and that in consequence he frequently became inincapable both physically and mentally. The minister calls in the man and says: I am told by four or five gentlemen of standing that you are in the habit of becoming incapable both physically and mentally by reason of the excessive use of intoxicating liquors; what are the facts? The applicant says:	There is not a word of truth in it;
I have been a total abstainer ever since I left the cradle. Very well, says the minister, I will appoint you as a pilot. He is appointed and takes a ship from Montreal down the St. Lawrence, but through an excessive use of intoxicants while on the boat he becomes incapable of navigating the ship, and the ship goes to the bottom. Suppose that these had beeh the facts in connection with the Empress of Ireland. I venture to say that in that case the indignation of the people of this country would have been so intense as to drive the Minister of Marine and Fisheries from public life for the rest of his days. *That would be an analogous case to the one now under discussion. The evidence shows that warning after warning had been given to the ex-Minister of Finance that Travers was a dishonest man, and

that he had been guilty of fraud and perjury. Mr. Fielding knew that, perhaps not actually but as a matter of law. Mr. Fielding would have known these facts if he had acted as a man of ordinary prudence would in dealing with his own personal affairs. If he had acted in this matter as I venture to say he would have acted had he been personally interested in it, he would have followed up these warnings and discovered the character of Travers, who was applying for the certificate. As I said the other day, Travers was in substance the Farmers Bank, and the ex-Minister of Finance the Treasury Board, and if the Hon. Mr. Fielding had followed up the warnings, as the learned commissioner said it was his duty to do, he would have discovered two things: First, that the subscribers to the capital stock of the Farmers Bank had not paid in $250,000 in cash; and secondly, the very much more important fact that Mr. Travers was a man who had been found guilty of both fraud and perjury. Here is the situation. You have the ex-Minister of Finance knowing as a matter of law, because he was bound to know what it was his duty to ascertain, that this man was guilty of fraud and perjury, and yet he puts him in a position where he had control of hundreds of thousands of dollars of the people for whom the ex-Minister of Finance was in a sense the trustee; so that you have a trustee guilty of a gross breach of trust. As I said the other day, I am not imputing any wilful wrong-doing to the ex-Minister of Finance. I am not saying that he actually knew these facts, but courts of law treat trustees as if they actually knew what it was their duty to ascertain. I will give an illustration, if I may be pardoned a personal reference. A short time ago I had a very important position to fill, and I was on the eve of appointing a gentleman who had been recommended to me, when it came to my ears as a rumour that this man was in the habit of getting on a spree and remaining there for two or three weeks at a time. I at once made an inquiry, and was satisfied that the rumour which had come to my ears was well founded. That man has not been appointed, and if the ex-Minister of Finance, in the interests of the public, had taken that sort of position, we would have had no such wrecking of the Farmers Bank as has caused so much loss and suffering to the people of this country.
Mr. FRANCIS N. MeCREA (Sherbrooke):
I had not intended to &ay anything on this question, but as it is of such an extraordinary nature I cannot allow it to pass without offering a few remarks. This legislation is extraordinary in more respects than one. There is no precedent for it either in this House nor, so far as I know, in any civilized country in the world. It is also extraordinary in respect of the parties who are the main movers in asking this House and the country to reimburse the depositors of the Farmers Bank. We are told that because the ex-Minister of Finance neglected his duty it is incumbent upon the Government to make good the losses *sustained. Before the late Government went out of office, this question came up in the House and was debated at some length, and I understand that some hon. gentlemen claimed on that occasion that the depositors should be reimbursed. With the exception of the letters of Leighton MeCarthy, the ex-Minister of Finance had reoeived no intimation beyond mere street gossip as to the condition of affairs in comr mention with the Farmers Bank.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
As the hon. gentleman was not in the House at that time, perhaps he will pardon me putting him right. As a matter of fact this House'had ordered the Finance Minister to bring down all the correspondence and papers in connection with the Farmers Bank, and we had before us then a book which I have here now containing all the correspondence; so that we had information at that time.
Mr. MeCREA: Not before the certificate was given.	*

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
Oh, no, but you were
referring to the discussion.
Mr. MeCREA; So far as I can gather from what has been said in the course of this debate the only written complaint made to the ex-Minister of Finance was by Leighton McCarthy, and when the ex-minister asked him to furnish details and full information Mr. McCarthy replied that the depositors with whom he was concerned had been satisfied, and consequently he would withdraw his charges. Outside of that, there is nothing beyond meeting the ex-Minister of Finance on the street corners and telling him to hold up the certificate. license had been issued before that protest was received, and, according to the opinion of Commissioner Meredith who investigated, could not be recalled by the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: The hon. gentleman has referred to a letter said to have been written by the ex-Finance Minister to Mr. McCarthy, asking him for particulars. Would he be kind enough to read that letter ? It was not brought down in the return. There is no such letter.

I said that Mr. McCarthy withdrew his charges, the parties for whom he was acting having been settled with. Consequently, he asked to have the document returned to him. That was the only written document I have heard mentioned here as having been put before the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: You only read part of it; read the whole letter.

This Government appointed a commissioner, a man of their own choosing, to hear the evidence both verbal and written. This commissioner has made his report. He exonerates the ex-Minister of Finance from any imputation of breach of faith, and winds up by saying that the most that could be charged against him is possibly an error of judgment. Now, if this Government are going to legislate that every time a minister of the Crown commits a probable error of judgment the country must pay for it, what will become of the country ? What will become of this country if the electors are going to be told that for every error of judgment that this Government may commit the country will have to be responsible and will have to pay ?
But a more extraordinary part of this question is this:	I was looking over the
list of the counties affected by this legislation, and I find that they number twenty-five. The Minister of Labour has told us that it was a part of the Conservative platform before the elections, and they made pledges and promises. Were those pledges and promises extended beyond the counties affected? I heard nothing of them in my county. No pledges were held out to the people of the province of Quebec that if the Conservatives were returned to power they would reimburse the depositors of the Farmers Bank. That goes to prove what we have always said-that this Government got into office by a combination of promises, each promise made to suit a locality.
A still further strange part of this legislation is the fact that the Finance Minister 
who brings it forward represents a county affected by this failure. It is true that he was returned in a by-election by acclamation and perhaps did not have to make any promises except to endorse those that had been made by others. But he realizes that he has to go back to his county for re-election and must redeem the pledges of his party before he does. In an ordinary case in court, say in a criminal case to be tried before a jury, if it can be shown that the parties summoned as jurymen are interested in the case, they are challenged for cause and ordered to stand aside and not allowed to serve; but we have twenty-five members sitting in this House who pledged themselves at the last election that if their party came into power they would implement these promises, right or wrong.
Name them.

Now, I am perhaps a
little old in years though young in politics; but my idea of this matter of politics has been that if a candidate holds out any promises or resorts to any corruption, he has to do it in such a way that the public will not hear or know of it, or he will be disqualified. But here we have a bunch of candidates, men who represent counties in this House, telling us that they have made promises	to their	constituents	in the
past and were elected on the strength of those	promises, and furthermore
telling us	that	if they	returnedto their	counties	without	fulfilling
their promises, they could not be re-elected. Not only have they made promises to the electors for the past election, but they are making further promises for a future election. This is something that ought to disqualify these men, in my way of thinking.
I do not like to be harsh, and if I did I do not know terms strong enough to condemn this legislation. If I were to use such terms as harsh as I think should be applied to such legislation, you would call me to order, Mr. Speaker, and you would probably be justified. This legislation is pernicious, it is wrong, and the generations not yet born will hear of it and suffer from it if it is put on the statute book.

1 do not wish to take more than a few moments, but I think the question is of sufficient importance to require fair discussion. I cannot quite agree with the reasons assigned by the hon. member for West Middlesex (Mr. Ross) for supporting this Bill. I cannot agree that merely

because there has been a great loss the country must come to the rescue of those who have lost. That is not good legislation unless we make it general. If the Government make a general declaration and say, we will recoup all depositors in banks that have failed, well and good. Nor do I accept the reasons given by the Minister of Finance as sufficient. He gives legal reasons, or what might be called legal reasons, why this should be done. As I understand the Minister of Finance, he would indicate that there is a legal responsibility resting upon Canada, unless we are relieved of that legal responsibility by some special rights which we have but which the ordinary individual does not have. I notice that in introducing this Bill he was asked by the leader of the Opposition:
Sir Wilfrid Laurier:	Are you going to proceed legally on this question?
Mr. White:	No, because, as I have said, the
negligence cannot be established as against the Crown, or as against a minister of the Crown acting in his capacity as minister. What I have sought to do is to show that on legal analogy the action of the Government is justifiable by reason of the fact that the negligence to which I have referred on the part of the Treasury Board was the primary and original cause of the loss of this money to the depositors.
In another place he says:
The Government's course is not based upon its legal liabilities, although I think on legal principles the Government is bound to reimburse these depositors.
He gives as a reason for that responsibility the fact, as he alleges, that the negligence to which I have referred on the pait of the Treasury Board was the primary and original cause of the loss of this moniv by the depositors. I am rather astonished that the minister should lay down the principle that the primary and original cause is necessarily a cause which would he sufficient to justify the court in find'.ng againsl the defendant, i think the principle of law is quite plain on the question of the sort of negligence which would entitle the court to give relief and I think I am right-in saying that the commissioner, from whom the minister quoted, never used the word ' negligence ' in connection with his refer ence to the board, and that therefore the minister has put in a term which the commissioner never used.
Not to take too much time with legal definitions, I think that all lawyers will agree with me that there must be some proximate or, as the commissioner says, efficient, cause of injury to enable the plaintiff to recover. That is a very different thing from the primary and original cause. A person who claims damages because of some primary and original cause generally fails because the damages are too remote. Some of us are accustomed to legal definitions as to what negligence there must be in order to bring a successful action. But let me read one or two:
The negligence must be the proximate cause of the injury.
And again:
The damage must be the legal and natural consequence of the word spoken or the action performed.
We know that the commissioner has found that the action of the department was not the proximate cause. He states himself clearly what the efficient cause, as he calls it, is, and he tells us that the efficient cause, the proximate cause, the thing which caused the damage, was t'he mismanagement of the bank and not the giving of the certificate.
Something has been said about the political reasons for this measure. I noticed in looking up a magazine friendly to the Government, a very sympathetic article on this Bill in which the writer lays the blame entirely on -the late Government, but he adds:
Then too, It must be remembered that the promise of restoring their money to the depositors was clearly made by the Conservatives in their election campaign in 1911.
That is the whole thing in a nutshell, and the hon. Minister of Labour (Mr. Crothers) pretty nearly puts it as strongly. The minister is putting the Bill before the House to carry out the promises which were made by the Ontario Conservative candidates, and we are told by the minister that they must redeem their pledges. I wonder how we in the West are going to come out. Does the same obliga-9 p.m. tion rest on the Government in regard to the natural resources of the West ? We have never heard anything about that. It seems to me that we have just as much right to have the promises made to us redeemed as the people of Ontario have. The present Government is certainly making a distinction all along in favour of the provinces that supported them against the provinces that opposed them, which is neither good legislation nor sound policy. There is one thing in the commissioner's report which has been referred to more than once in this House;

that is where the commissioner speaks of an error of judgment. He says:
The most that can properly be charged against the Department of Finance or the Treasury Board is an error of judgment.
The Minister of Finance, in his speech when introducing this Bill, said that this remark was made in reference to the charge of fraud in obtaining the certificate. If T am wrong the minister can correct me, but he certainly said in his speech that this remark of the commissioner was made in reference to the charge of improper action in obtaining the certificate. Let us look at that matter. As you will find on pages 8 and 9 of his report, the commissioner deals with the fact that Mr. Travers had made an improper statement which had led the Treasury Board to believe that certain moneys were paid in cash which were not as a matter of fact paid in cash. The commissioner deals very fully with that, then goes on to deal with the other matter to which the minister has referred, and then sums up in regard to everything with the words which I have used:
The most that can properly be charged against the Department of Finance or the Treasury Board is an error of judgment.
I think my hon. friend will see that that remark of the commissioner must have referred to their action in not making what he considered sufficient investigation. How could it possibly refer to the charge of fraud, how could it possibly refer to the charge that some one had been approached and bought up ? Let us look at what he says in regard to that:
An unsuccessful attempt was made to show that money had been used by Travers to procure the issue of the certificate.
My hon. friend the Minister of Finance told us that the statement of the commissioner in regard to an error of judgment referred to this. Would this be an error of judgment even if the statement were true ? If it were not true, where is the error of judgment ? The error of judgment could have no possible connection with that, and the minister knows it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Read the paragraph.

I will read the whole thing:
As I have already pointed out, Travers in his reply did not give the assurance for which the minister had asked, viz., an assurance that nothing of the kind had taken place in relation to the subscriptions for the Farmers Bank, but that the amounts set forth in the application as

having been paid up have in every case been bona fide cash payments.
Unfortunately, Travers' reply appears to have been treated by the department as containing the assurance for which the minister had asked.
I very much doubt whether in the circumstances it would have been right to have depended upon the word of Travers, even if he had given the assurance for which the minister had asked. The information which had been conveyed to the minister had come from gentlemen of standing, and if it was accurate the declaration Travers had made was untrue, and it would seem to have been almost an idle thing to ask for an assurance that there was no foundation for the statements that had been made to the minister from the very man whose honesty was in question, and unwise to have acted on that assurance.
It is true that, as Mr. Fielding stated in evidence, Travers, so far as he knew, was a reputable banker; but that was not, in my opinion, a sufficient reason for not having instituted an inquiry as to the matters which had been called to his attention. Such an inquiry could easily have been made, and the delay occasioned by it would have been inconsiderable, and such an inquiry would, undoubtedly, have resulted in the discovery of the manner in which the $100,000 had been raised and in the refusal of the Treasury Board to give the certificate.
An unsuccessful attempt was made to show that money had been used by Travers to procure the issue of the certificate. In support of it Travers testified to the issue of a cheque for $3,000 which he said was placed in an envelope addressed to Mr. Peter Ryan and sent to Mr. Ryan's room in the Russell House, at Ottawa, and afterwards presented and cashed.
That Ryan received this cheque or had any connection with it if it was used for the purpose stated by Travers, was disproved.
There is, in my opinion, no ground for supposing that any improper influence was used to induce the Treasury Board to give the certificate or to induce the Minister of Finance to recommend the granting of it, and the most that can properly be charged against the Department of Finance or the Treasury Board is an error of judgment.
How can the minister say that this error of judgment had any connection whatever with the charge of fraud? Fraud and error of judgment are two entirely distinct-things. Any one knows that this statement of the commissioner refers to the first part of the complaint, not to the fraud. Surely the minister knows that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I did not intend to say anything to the contrary. I did not allege it was fraud.
' Mr. THOMSON: The minister said most positively, in introducing this Bill, that the remark regarding the error of judgment had reference to the charge of fraud.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It follows immediately upon what was stated.
It follows immediately upon both statements, and it is a summing up. I grant that the paragraphing of this part of the report is not very good.
That is a pity.

The minister has tried to convey the impression that there would be a legal liability on a private individual under similar circumstances. Let us deal with the remark of the commissioner that the most that can properly be said in regard to this is that it is an error of judgment. Can the minister show us a judgment delivered by any judge in the civilized world in which he has stated that a matter is an error of judgment and in which he has then found for the plaintiff? He cannot do it. The finding of the commissioner is that at the worst it is an error of judgment.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Would my hon. friend read that again? The error of judgment, as I understand it, related to the action of the Department of Finance. In another part the commissioner finds that it was incumbent upon the Treasury Board to do something which it did not do, aamely, to hold an inquiry.
The commissioner refers both to the minister and the Department of Finance.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: He refers to the Department of Finance?

The commissioner says:
The most that can properly be charged against the Department of Finance or the Treasury Board is an error of judgment.
Does the minister seriously intend to recoup the people of Canada for every error of judgment made my himself and his predecessors? If not, where does the Government stand in regard to the matter? I believe the Government were guilty of a very serious error of judgment when, last fall, they did not place wheat on the free [DOT]list, and in that way take advantage of the opportunity which the United States gave them, lit would have saved millions to the people of Canada if they had done so.
Is that an error of judgment on their part?

The minister said most positively:
No certificate-no bank and no Travers-no bank or no Travers- no loss to depositors.
That has been dealt with somewhat by my hon. friend from Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair), and I do not want to go into that any further.
My impression is that the minister has not the power to insist upon a certain person being placed in charge of a bank. If I am wrong, the minister can correct me. Then how could the department have insisted that Travers should not have been engaged? There is no question that the directors would have re-engaged Travers, even if his actions had been brought to their attention, because they knew what he had done. There was not an act that Travers had done up to that time of which the directors who appointed him were hot cognizant. I do not know if we are to take action against the directors to recover what the depositors have lost. Surely the directors are more responsible than the Department of Finance, if it is a matter of Travers being engaged.
It is quite plain that it is not because of any obligation, moral or legal, that is resting upon this Government that this Bill is introduced. I can imagine very well that the minister, every night before he retires to his peaceful couch, utters a very serious prayer that the 'Senate may come to his relief and throw this Bill out.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Oh, no.

Whether the Senate will pull his chestnuts out of the fire or not remains to be seen. I cannot imagine for a moment that the minister really wants this Bill to become liaw. I cannot imagine he has so little regard for what should be on the statute-books of Canada as to want that, and I think those of us who have the interest of the country at heart will vote against this Bill.
Amendment (Mr. Sinclair) negatived, on division.
Bill read the third time and passed, on division.

I desire to get some
information with regard to a proposed diversion of the Intercolonial, and the surveys made. I desire to know if the survey parties examined the proposed diversion running from ILinwood through Cape Jack and the village of Harbour au Bouche. A petition was sent to the Government some time ago from the residents of that place, praying for this diversion, and it was sent to the department. I do not know how the department is disposed to view it. Speaking generally, that portion of the eastern extension from New Glasgow to the strait of Canso, goes through the very poorest part of the country. I do not know how it was, but when that road was run regard seems to have been had to the engineering or to the contractor's interest rather than to the convenience of the people, particularly from Linwood to Mulgrave, distant two or three miles from the village of Harbour au Bouche. That village is one of the prettiest places in the eastern part of Nova Scotia, a thriving fishing village where considerable business is done. A strange thing is that when the road was built it did not go through the village. The proposition is to run from Linwood through - Cape Jack and Harbour au Bouche. I ob-

served from the papers that were brought down in response to a motion made by myself some time ago, that in 1890 an application was made for this diversion. A survey was made on that occasion and a report presented which, I confess, when I read it, I thought a startling report.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: What is the date of it?

It is dated October 1, 1892. This was when Sir John Thompson represented Antigonish. It was at his request that the survey was made. I observe that there was considerable delay in having it made. There did'not appear to be any desire at Moncton to comply with the prayer of the petitions sent in by residents of the district referred to. A letter of the 2nd September, 1892, says:
Have the survey made at once, as promised by the minister, no delay admissible.
So the survey was made, and, under date of October 1, 1892, Mr. P. S. Archibald reports as follows:
Oct. 1st, 1892.
D. Pottinger, Esq.,
Chief Superintendent,
Moncton.
Dear Sir,-As instructed by Mr. Schreiber's letter of the 19th August last, I have had a survey made for the proposed diversion of the line via Harbour au Bouche Village, and under another cover I enclose you plans and profiles. I also enclose herewith an estimate of the cost, amounting to $62,273.39. Instead of shortening the line as was supposed, it will lengthen it by the blue line 4.14 miles, and by the red line 3.54 miles. The gradients you will observe too, by the profile, are very unfavourable. I have not considered it worth while to lay down the location, or send you a profile of the red line; I can do so if you wish.
Yours truly,
(Sgd.) P. S. Archibald.
Then there was a detailed statement of the cost. I call the attention of the acting minister to this report, as he might be inclined to think that the change proposed is not in the interest of the road as such, and does not meet the requirements of the people in this district. The report says that the line will not be shortened. I was surprised at that. But even if the distance were a little longer, it is only three or four miles. But the report says also that the gradients would be very unfavourable. Of course, we must treat with due respect the reports of engineers, but I am sure the people down there will find it hard to believe that they could not run a line from Linwood through Cape Jack and Harbour au Bouche without getting better grades and curves than those in the present road. It

does seem to me, in reading the correspondence, observing the delay in making the survey, the tone of the report and other things-reading between the lines-there was no desire at that time to make the change. There seemed to be a disposition to switch off the application. I can understand that. At that time the traffic was comparatively small and the revenues of the road were very much lower than they are to-day. The department would consider an expenditure of	$62,000 or thereabouts wasted	if	it were merely
to improve the railway accommodation for the people at that time. Things have changed, however, and I hope that the minister will not be influenced in any way by the report which was made in 1892. I hope that the survey parties now working on the Intercolonial railway will make a careful survey with a view to meeting the wishes of the people in those districts. I feel confident that if a careful survey is made, a good line will be obtained which will be of great convenience to the people. I do not wish to take up the time of the committee in elaborating on the character of the country and the improved facilities which this change would give; the facts are correctly set forth in the petition which is before the minister. This change would effect another improvement in that there is a bad grade between Linwood and a point some miles east of Harbour au Bouche. I would like to ask the minister if he knows whether the survey parties have dealt with the matter referred to in the petition of the residents of Linwood and Harbour au Bouche-

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: I cannot say whether or not there is a survey party in that district at the present time. I do know, however, that the general manager has survey parties out along the Intercolonial railway, who are working with a view to improving grades along the line. It may be necessary at some points to divert the road from its present course; as I understand it, at the place mentioned by my hon. friend it may be necessary, in order to carry out his wishes, that a diversion of the road be made. However, when the survey parties have completed all the necessary work along the line, this matter will be considered and everything will be done which is necessary to improve the roadbed of the Intercolonial railway.

The management of Intercolonial railway have decided
to put an additional train on the line during the coming summer season. This train, I understand, will be composed exclusively of sleeping cars for the benefit of passengers going to the various summer resorts along the St. Lawrence. There is going to be one sleeper for Riviere Ouelle, another for Rivifere du Loup, another for C'acouna, another for Bic and Rimouski and another for Little Metis. I do not object to the running of this train; I think it will be a great improvement, but the people of the village of Kamouraska are complaining that this will discriminate against one of the finest summer resorts on the St. Lawrence river. I think that there are more tourists summering at Kamouraska than there are at any of the points that are to be served by this train called the St. Lawrence Special. I would ask the minister to use his influence with the manager of the Intercolonial railway with a view to having another sleeper put on this train for St. Paschal, where passengers for Kamouraska get off. St.. Paschal is the county town of the riding; it has a population of over 3,000 people and these people certainly deserve to have a sleeper put on the train for this place. I would call the attention of the minister to a statement made by his manager and published in the newspapers recently to the effect that the best paying section of the Intercolonial is that between Levis and Riviere du Loup, so that I hope the department will not be discriminatory in this matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext:
As 1 understand the' hon.
gentleman, he wishes another sleeper put on the train from Montreal east to St. Paschal.

For the benefit of
Kamouraska.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext:
Surely the Intercolonial in
running trains from Montreal east will put on a sleeper at any time, if there are a sufficient number of passengers to justify their doing so.

This is a new train,
and there is no sleeper for the section of the country to which I have referred. The train is going to run three days, in the week going down and three days in the week coming up. It is especially on Friday nights going down and Sunday nights coming up that it would be convenient for passengers to and from Kamouraska to have a sleeper on the train.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: I shall be very glad to take the matter up with the general manager with a view to seeing whether the wishes of the hon. member can be carried out.

I believe that under
this item we are to discuss the Trent Valley Canal report. On account of the illness of Mr. Stratton, the former member for Peterborough, I had no intention of bringing the matter up, but members of the Opposition have seemed to think it desirable that the matter should be discussed; therefore I have much pleasure in complying with their request.
The report which was made on the investigation at the instance of the Department of Railways and Canals disclosed a most extraordinary state of affairs in the Trent district. It showed not only looseness but corruption. I have the opinion that those who have been, as it were, caught in the act, those who have been the instruments of this corruption, are not most to blame. I propose to show that the whole tenor of the conduct of affairs in the administration in the Trent canal in the Peterborough district wras of such a character that no employee could hold his job and not do what he was told to do by those in authority over him, who demanded that he should do as they wished, and what they wished was corrupt from top to bottom. I have no desire to make any political capital out of this matter. I do not think that the Liberal party as a party can be blamed for what took place at Peterborough; it was rather due to the general frailty of human nature. Several Conservatives were mixed up in the matter, which shows the complete impartiality of the report and of the manner in which the investigation was made.
One of the most extraordinary things connected with this whole affair from beginning to end was the giving away by the Liberal Government of a property valued at $500,000 for one dollar a year for fifty years to a band of favourites. That, I think, is enough to show anybody the character of the administration of the Trent Valley canal. I shall now proceed to show more in detail what that means. On the main line of the Trent waterway at a place called Burleigh falls, where there is a fall about twenty-eight feet high-that is the height of the locks-there is a magnificent water-power. With the exception of the water-power at Healey falls it is without doubt the finest water-power on the whole Trent system and is a morsel

on which engineers had been looking for many years. Some years ago I asked an eminent New York electrical engineer who happened to be in the neighbourhood what power could be developed cheaply at Burleigh falls. He said:	Considering the extent of the fore bay, the steadiness of the flow, etc., as well as the height of the falls, I should say that not less than 6,000 horse-power at minimum flow; but of course you can, on account of the character of the neighbourhood, at very little expense, raise that to at least 8,000 horse-power, that would be an easy matter. The most unpractised eye could see that this is the case, the water flows from Lovesick lake into Stoney lake and in its passage flows over Burleigh falls, and also through two small streams called Perry's creek. These are the three means of escape for the water into Stoney lake. The main course of the stream falling into Stoney lake is dammed back for the purposes of navigation by a Government dam which cost a very large amount. I am within the mark when I say that it cost $100,000; I think it cost much more. The Government have to maintain that dam and to keep the water at this height in order to make the waterpower at Burleigh falls a very remunerative affair, all that has to be done is to build across the apertures of PeTry's creek two short dams, and I am within the mark when I say they can be built for $5,000 apiece at the very outside. The cost of development of the water-power, of course, would vary according to t'he amount of power you wish to develop. The full development of 6,000 horse-power could be attained by an expenditure, all told, of $30,000. So that the gift by the Government to this private company of this waterpower at Burleigh falls was a gift of 6,000 horse-power at minimum flow at one dollar a year for fifty years, which would cost them $30,000. The lease was made by the late Hon. A. G. Blair when he was Minister of Railways. It was confirmed by the late Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham), that is the assignment was confirmed, in 1910.
The assignment to whom?

The assignment in trust to Ewing and Ross, the assignment of the lease. The history of this was that Mr. Blair really did not want to grant this lease; he suspected that it was not right and did not want to grant it. But, what

are you going to do when men high in the councils of the Liberal party write letters demanding practically that this be done? The Central Ontario Power Company, Limited, which took over this property irom Culverwell, or which he concocted for the purpose of taking it over, had amongst its stockholders the Hon. Richaid Har-court, late Minister of Education at Toronto, who had $10,000 stock. Then we had also the late Postmaster General, Sir William Mulock. Sir William Mulock wrote:
With further reference to the application of J. A. Culverwell for a water-power privilege in the county of Victoria, I think on the line of the Trent canal, after careful conisderation and full inquiry I recommend this application to your favourable consideration.
Yours truly,
W. Mulock.
Hon. Richard Harcourt, at one time Minister of Education for Ontario, writes:

Dear Mr. Blair,
In the application of J. Alexander Culverwell of Toronto on Buleigh falls, kindly see correspondence. Our arrangements can be completed and satisfactorily closed on Monday provided we hear from you tomorrow. New York bankers-
New York bankers? New York grandmothers, the whole thing was being managed by friends of the Government in Canada:
New York bankers will be in Toronto on Monday to close but nothing can be done until we hear from you. Will you wire J. Alexander Culverwell on Monday sure. I may not be in Toronto until Thursday evening.
Yours truly,	*
R. Harcourt.
P.S.-I am personally interested in the matter.
These are the eminent gentlemen who are looking after the interests of the country. Mr. Harcourt writes again:
Dear Mr. Blair,	.
Mr. J. Alexander Culverwell of Toronto, an electrical engineer, has had some correspondence with your office late last February and since that time. It is important that his application shall be disposed of. I am interested in the company he is forming and will be glad if you will settle up the matter.
Certainly, he has $10,000 stock in it, which got its value by the late Government giving away the property of the people of this country, and he proposes to realize on it as soon as possible. Is it any wonder that the poor wretches employed on the Trent Valley canal think they might get a few rake-offs of candles, cigars and bottles of whisky when a no/ble example like this
is set them. My respect for these gentlemen is an inverse ratio to the amounts they get out of the swindle. Sir William Mulock writes to Mr. Blair as follows:
Dear Mr. Blair,
In case this 'matter may have escaped your attention I desire to remind you that I will be glad if you can make a satisfactory arrangement with Mr. Culverwell.
Senator McHugh also had to have a finger in the pie. He wrote:
I have had a request to urge on the department the completion of an arrangement with Mr. J. A. Culverwell. The delay is hindering the organization of the company. I would be pleased to have this matter receive your early attention.
Then, the mayor of Lindsay and George McHugh, the senator, also concocted an epistle which they forwarded to Mr. Blair. Mr. Blair agreed, and handed over this magnificent asset to J. Alexander Culverwell, who is about as astute a, man as I know, and to the Central Ontario Power [DOT]Company, which, of course, consisted of a lot otf financial giants, including the Hon. Richard Harcourt. Let us look at the lease. The date of authorization was November 4, 1899. (The hon. member read part of the lease.) This asset was ultimately assigned to the Central Ontario Power Company, and then bonded to Ewing and Ross under a total bondage of $760,000.
This iniquity could not have been perpetrated except with the consent of the Minister of Railways and Canals. This magnificent water-power is given away for fifty years for the magnificent sum of one dollar a year, and we may not even get that by the provisions of the last clause I have read. The lease allows damage if not unnecessary. Of course, any lawyer knows that if damage were done and it could be shown that it was not unnecessary it would be like the Farmers Bank-away she goes. The Government of this country proposes to hand over this magnificent water-power to this company for the sum of one dollar a year. Is it any wonder that the people of this country are beginning to get tired of the way they are being treated? It is hardly possible that this kind of thing can go on. That is the state of affairs along the Trent Valley canal and it is something we should take cognizance of.
But how is it with the poor creatures who have perhaps taken a little more than they should have, infringed the moral law or done something of that sort? These poor

wretches are all suspected. They have all got into serious trouble, their last hope is about gone. The man who used to represent Peterborough but who now, unfortunately, is ill, and who should have looked after the interest of that district, suffered this to go on. Yet, I do not find any recommendation for his suspension in the report, and in that respect the report is astray. The report also shows that as to the pay sheet some very strange things have happened. There was a Miss Carr, who was employed in the office of A. H. Stratton and E. S. Clarry, one the brother of the Hon. Mr. Stratton, who used to represent West Peterborough, and the other the Government accountant at the Trent Valley Canal office. This girl was put on the Government pay-list as a labourer. She was down on the pay-list as having worked on the dam, as having shoved logs about, as having done some of the things which only a big husky man could do, something which she as a matter of fact had never done. But she was put down as a labourer on the pay-list in order to pay an account contracted by Messrs. Stratton and Clarry; the pay-sheet was put through the Government office here, and the pay was extracted from the treasury and handed over to these gentlemen to pay their account with. I believe it is understood that prosecution is to follow. All these cases must unquestionably be run down; public opinion demands it. I hope the minister is listening. These cases must be followed up to the bitter end. It is intolerable that the treasury of the country should be rifled in this manner and the culprits escape. We find that one Clark, who was an accountant of Mr. J. R. Stratton in the Peterborough Examiner office, was put on the pay-list as another man w'orking out in the country on the dams, with saw-logs and all the rest of it, and Mr. Stratton's accounts were paid by means of this false pay-sheet. Mr. Stratton was liable for $2,000 a day for allowing that to go on while sitting as a member of this House and the consequence is that his estate will no doubt be requested to hand over a certain sum to make up that deficiency. It will be an extraordinary thing if it is not.
From the date of the Gamey transaction, the Farmers Bank and the Burleigh Falls scandal, Peterborough has been dragged in the mud and blazoned all over this blooming country as the centre of folly and fraud. I wish to say that the people of Peterborough are really, for the most part, a decent and

respectable people. It is true that there are some people amongst them who belong to the Conservative party, or say they do, for political purposes or financial purposes, who transfer their allegiance when necessary to the Liberal party, and that there are members of the Liberal party who, when necessary, will transfer their apparent allegiance to the Conservative party. The two sets of men acting together, by reason of their political influence, turn the keys in the door of favouritism on the part of the leaders of both parties. That is the way the thing is worked. We have people like that in Peterborough. We have a lot of people-there is no question about that-who are perfectly satisfied if they can only make, a few dollars illegally, or improperly. If they can get a few bottles of 11 p.m. whisky from the Government or steal a few sandwiches or cigars, they are perfectly happy because they do not have to pay for them.
And you call them decent people ?
No, I say these are not decent people. I am very pleased to think that the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Gauvreau) has such a lively sense of what is right.

That is what you said.
Mr. 'BURNHAM: I know, and I am very glad to see that the hon. member observed it. I have as much respect as anybody for the ex-Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham1) and I do not wish to say anything unbecoming of him. I believe that he does what he thinks best for the interests of the country, but he and the Hon. Mr. Blair were both deceived. The iniquity was originated and perpetrated at Peterborough. If at the present time a state of things such as this could transpire, while I am representing Peterborough, I would be to blame and I would be willing to take the blame. I do not wish to transfer the blame to other people's shoulders. When I came in, I found among other things, that there had been concocted what I would call the rottenest sort of graft on a small scale that I have ever seen. The Government pays once a month, about the fifteenth, so that if you are a casual employee and have earned any money you have to wait until the Government cheque comes in before you can get your pay. A great many of these poor men have been perhaps a long time out of employment, they have little saved, their families are large, they want their money in the very

worst way, and a dollar bill in ready money looks as big as ten if you have to wait for it. I found that some men in this Trent Valley Canal office were taking powers of attorney from these poor wretches, going to the bank, shaving their notes and handing these poor devils the balance. I said:	I will crucify you if you do not
stop that. I said:	It is a cruel, rotten
system and it must be stopped. They lied about it when I asked them whether they were still doing it; they said no, that they had stopped it. I went to the bank and asked the bank about it. They said that it was perfectly wrong. I had hard work to get the head office here to believe it. They said:	It is impossible, because we
have provided a fund for that purpose. I sent a wire to the office here saying:	I
have a case now; come at once. Down came the auditor and he found that what I had told him was perfectly true. When I made complaints I could not get these complaints acted upon, because these rascals at Peterborough would know three or four days after I had made the complaint that I had made it. The whole thing was headed off and I could not do anything. In the Times newspaper of Peterborough of February 8, 1909, there is an article eulogizing Mr. Graham, the late Minister of Railways and Canals, for his railway management. The proprietors of the newspaper are put on the pay sheet of the department, to pay for the article, so the Government paid for it. That is just a little instance, but it shows how these things are done. They go on the pay sheet as labourers. No investigation is held. If you happen to be rascal enough to have contrived a system of powers of attorney, you can forge any one's name you like, because, When the evidence is taken respecting the power of attorney and it is asked:	Is this the case
to which it applied? the man who gave the power of attorney knows nothing about it. The whole thing is concocted in such a way that it is impossible to deal with it, and the system of rascality becomes so general that it cannot be uncovered. This Government, and this Parliament, may consider themselves lucky that Mr. Ferguson was able to find out as much as he did.
It cost a lot of money.

Yes, it cost a lot of money. Possibly the hon. member for Prescott begrudges the spending of that
money; he would like to see this rascality go on and this country soaked and sucked of the last dollar that it has rather than that this money should be spent.
He is not so bad as that.
Oh, no.
It could have been unearthed by an official of the department.

My hon. friend objects to the unearthing. He objects to the facts, simply because an employee of the department has not unearthed them. What has that to do with the matter? When a murder is committed, the deed is done; the unearthing of the murderer does not prevent the crime from having been committed. There is no use in putting up such excuses as that, because I am not going to be bluffed by them.
I do not mean to say that Mr. Ferguson should not have been appointed as commissioner.
We will appoint you as commissioner.
We are objecting to the expenditure of $900.

Well, then, I will pay back the $900 if you think it should be done.
The statement was made that this canal management in Peterborough was not being run as a political concern; that that part of the report was entirely uncalled-for and improper. I think I can enlighten the House in that respect. Mr. Stratton was the member, and in 1909 he wrote certain lettrs. (The hon. member then read the letters).
What could poor McClellan do in the face of Mr. Stratton's letter, but give this man an order? He is a member of the Conservative organization in Peterborough, and was always considered a good Conservative. Therefore, this order must be all the more promptly fulfilled, if it was going [DOT] to do any good before the election-' a bumper one for the election '-that sounds good. It speaks for itself, as Mr. Stratton says, and I think it does.
There was a letter from Mr. Stratton under date of April 17, 1909, as a consequence of which they went and interviewed Mr. Brown. You may well fancy that a lot of things were done which would affect Mr. McClellan's conscience, and possibly Mr. Stratton's ,and possibly Mr. Brown's.

Nevertheless who would get the blame? Poor McClellan would get every bit of it; but I am trying t-o give Mr. Stratton some of it now.
On the 10th of July, 1909, he writes Mr. McClellan again. This is rather curious, because these letters are all marked personal. They were put on Mr. McClellan's personal file; Mr. McClellan gave me his order to get the file, and I have the information first-hand. These lettre were not intended for the public file. They are all marked personal. I have the written permission of Mr. McClellan, who owns these letters, to read them.
Do you think it is fair to read a personal private letter? I appeal to the honesty of the hon. member.

Seeing that he has
given me permission to read them, I think it is perfectly fair.
It is only a question of honesty.
I am glad to see that my hon. friend thinks the letters are pretty damaging.

They may damage
yourself.
It is the reading of them that is damaging.
When I get letters and am authorized to use them, I think I am at perfect liberty to do so.
What about the sender?
The sender does not own a letter after it is sent.
It is a matter of taste.
Yee, it is a matter of taste. In this case it is also a matter of smell.	*
What does the minister think?

The minister has
nothing to do with it. These letters are owned by Mr. McClellan.
A lot of work was done by way of dredging in the slip at Peterborough that had no more to do with the canal than this House has, and an immense sum of money was spent. Here are letters from Mr. Stratton telling Mr. McClellan to go on and have these things done and to hurry them up. One day I sent word to the

department asking them if they intended to allow the country to be bled continually by all these thieves and robbers connected with the whole system there, or if they were going to try to stop it. A question was put on the Order Paper, and the whole thing was closed down in five minutes. I never saw anything stop so quickly. There was never another shovelful taken out. They had been digging out this private slip at immense expense. They raised the dam to make a higher head for a private company. That is the sort of stuff that poor McClellan is blamed for. I just wish to point these things out, because we must do some sort of justice to poor McClellan.
I have spoken of Miss Carr. It cannot be denied that Miss Carr's name was repeatedly put on the pay-list-in November, December, April, January, August, September, October, 1907-8-for the purpose of payments of this kind. She was put on as a ' labourer ' and was paid sums of $6.25, $4, $5, $6, and so on. Of course, she never got a cent of it. But I think the most barefaced thing that was done was the putting on the accountant in Stratton's own office, to be paid as a labourer on the Trent canal. I have no time or inclination to go into all these bills about liquors and cigars, and all that rot. That is bad enough. We have the time checks. I was very much amused at the time checks of Robert Shaw. He is warden of the county and also reeve of the township of Harvey. He was put on as labourer at several places that are a long, long way from where he lives or ever worked. But I have no doubt he got his pay; he would be hardly likely to allow his name to go on a thing in which there was money and not get it. That is the kind of gum-game they played. A little authentic evidence is advisable, and as I happen to have it by me I would like to give you the benefit of it. I do not wish to take up too much time-
Hear, hear.

I have no doubt the
hon. gentleman finds it too much.
I am not alone. Ask the ministers.

I have here extracts
from the report of the Privy Council in reference te the lease. I have also the assignment of the Central Ontario Power Company to Ewing and Ross, which was approved and confirmed by the exjMinister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham), continuing the lease at one dollar per annum

'and involving a total of $750,000. Now let me say, had the property at Burleigh falls been turned to the public account, it would have netted at that time all that these men expected to make out of it, which, as you see, was not less than $500,000. Fortunately, the present Minister of Railways (Mr. Cochrane) came and stood upon the dam at Burleigh falls and I pointed this matter out to him and said:	Surely, you
are not going to allow this thing to go on, he said: Certainly not; this is fraud of the first water, and I will have it cancelled immediately, and he gave an order that nothing was to be allowed to be done with the lease of that property, and nothing has been done since. So that sum has been saved there. When a few hundred dollars damages are paid around the neighbourhood and the water was raised, as it must be raised for the immense new lock that is to be built there, the old lock would have furnished excellent wheel pits.
Is the minister making any use of it now?

No, but I will tell you what is going to happen:	this is being
handed over by the Dominion to the HydroElectric Commmission of Ontario and the Hydro-Elecrtic Commission is going to make use of it.
What authority is there for that statement?
Mr. Beck.

It has been denied in
this House.
All I can say is that Mr. Beck says he is getting it.
And the Government has denied it.

I cannot help that.
But that is merely a matter of detail. The point is that it has been taken out of the hands of private parties and restored to the public domain. I may be in error about a few details; I am not in the confidence of the minister. Mr. Beck told me in the precincts of this House, and I know from both sides that he is now taking an account of the property of the Seymour Power Company and about thirty others, in order that the Hydro-Electric may buy out the whole system of power in the Trent district and furnish hydro-electric power to the people of that district as they are furnishing it elsewhere.

I think you will find
that matter is in the courts-a part of it at least.

This I will say, and I think the hon. gentleman will agree with me
that Burleigh falls should never have been handed over by the Government to private parties at one dollar a year. That is the gravamen of my case-that when the late Government handed over to private parties for fifty years at a dollar a year, this enormous water-power, they simply betrayed the people of this country. Innocently or otherwise, if you like. I do not wish as I say, to make a charge of moral obliquity because I do not believe any exists here. I do not believe that Mr. Blair or Mr. Graham would do it, but when people make money and you do not know how they make it; there is a nigger in the woodpile.
What was the date of the lease for fifty years?
It began in 1899; the date of the lease is February 2, 1900, and it was to continue until 1959.
Does my hon. friend say that the minister was at liberty to cancel this lease and take the property back any time he pleased?
No.
How did he manage to do it?
If I were minister and you walked off with $500,000 or $600,000 worth of property and I were told that it was given to you, I would take it away from you.
I suppose the minister sat on the dam, waived his hand, and the property came back. I wanted to know how he got it.

When there was a rumour afloat that for legal reasons they were about to make a beginning at the development, officials of the Government were sent to stop it; not to allow it to proceed under any consideration. Hon. gentlemen will find that magnificent waterpower, putting it at the lowest estimate was worth $10 a year clear profit for 6,000 horse-power at the minimum flow of water, or $60,000 a year for fifty years.

My hon. friend has
spoken at some length, and with a great deal of heat, but he has kept away very

largely from the subject that I thought he was going to discuss, the report of the commissioner. He has dealt altogether with Burleigh falls, in respect of which a lease was made some fifteen or sixteen years ago.
I do not recall the circumstances connected with this lease, but I may mention the fact that fifteen or sixteen years ago waterpower in the Trent district, where these Burleigh falls are, was not considered of very great value. Men who looked further ahead than, perhaps, some other people, had gone up to the Trent district as well as through other districts and got control of a great many water-powers. The result is that this lease was given to a man named Culverwell, I understand, on condition that he give up claim to other powers he had secured. The Ontario Government some years ago practically gave up many of the rights they had along the Trent Valley system to the Dominion Government toy Order in Council, making no mention about retaining any rights to any of the water-powers. The reason why they did so was that they had bben compelled to maintain the dams to make provisions whereby lumbermen could float their logs. Ultimately, by Order in Council, the provincial Government turned over to the Dominion Government certain rights along the Trent Valley system and this Government took control of it from that time for the purposes of the Trent canal. The last right that the Ontario Government had was in respect of Healey's falls, and they leased that right to this same Culverwell when the present Minister of Bailways was Minister of Lands and Mines. When the time came that this Government proceeded to develop the power along that line, the lease was cancelled by the Ontario Government; and we had to make some settlement, and it was with the same Culverwell. I point out these facts merely to show that these water-powers years ago were not considered to be as valuable as they are now deemed to be. That, however, has nothing to do with the report of the commissioner, Mr. Ferguson. It is alleged that these people were put on the pay-roll for certain purposes. They knew nothing about their names being put on the pay-roll; they got checks, and swear that they performed the services for which they -were paid.
