Intercolonial railway-working expenses,

Air. BOUiLAY (Rimouski): (Translation..) Air. Chairman, considering the lateness of the hour, it is not my intention to retain the committee very long. I wish to offer a few remarks concerning the management of the Government railway, having been for a number of years connected with the running of that railway line, and, for the last forty years, having been living in the valley of the Alatapedia, through which the Intercolonial runs over a distance exceeding one hundred and twenty miles. When I settled in that valley about thirty years ago, the fine parishes which may be seen to-day along the line of the Intercolonial had just been opened. I witnessed the growth of these thriving settlements, as a consequence of the building of the railway. As I stated previously, I have been myself an employee of the Intercolonial for about ten years,
and then a patron of the road for a great number of years.
I am thoroughly acquainted with the working of the whole Intercolonial system, having taken a deep interest in the matter. What I propose doing to-night is to disclose a state of things which is not generally known in the country, for if the facts were known to the public and at headquarters in Ottawa, I am satisfied that the province of Quebec would obtain, fairer treatment.
The province of Quebec is being discriminated against to an extraordinary extent in connection with the management of the Intercolonial. That condition of things has lasted forty years. Unfortunately very few people of influence have spoken out in vindication of the rights of the province of Quebec as regards the management of the Intercolonial. When that line of railway was built through the. Matapadia valley, there was, as I have stated, only a very sparse settlement along the line, and of course the influence these settlers exerted was restricted in proportion to their numbers. But to-day the population of that district reaches 25,000 or 30,000 souls, and it has the right to claim fair treatment from the managers of the railway.
In order that hon. gentlemen may fully realize to what extent we are being discriminated against, I may say that the mileage of the Intercolonial in the province of Quebec is 491 miles; that is more than half the total length of the main line. Of course, that railway, all told, has a mileage of 1,467 miles, but that includes all the branch lines. There are then 491 miles of that railway line in the province of Quebec. That means incidentally that in the matter of the manning of that railway, we are far from getting the consideration to which we are entitled on the basis of population. The Maritime provinces, including New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island, have a total population of 1,150,000, while the province of Quebec has a population of over two millions, which means a difference in our favour of eight or nine hundred thousand souls. That would entitle us to an equal share, to say the least, of the patronage in connection with that line. Now we shall see that the province of Quebec is far from receiving that proportion, and people will thus realize what treatment has been dealt out to us by the management of the Intercolonial within the lust forty years. That condition of things has never been properly brought to light,

but I hope that my statement of the case will induce those who are in control of the road to seriously consider the matter.
In order to collect further data, I asked several questions during this session, and the answers given enable me to supply some interesting particulars. For instance, I inquired what was last year the amount of traffic on that railway in the province of Quebec, between Campbellton and Montreal; what was the proportion of that same traffic for the Maritime provinces, from Campbellton to Halifax, exclusive of Prince Edward Island. The answer I received was not what I asked for, since it pointed out the amount of the traffic for the month of December, 1913, only, and not for the whole year. That statement does not impart a correct idea of the traffic of the province of Quebec during the whole year, especially as regards the valley of the Matapedia, between Campbellton and Ste. Flavie. That is the period of the year when traffic is at its lowest, as it consists in the main of shipments of lumber, of which a very small quantity is shipped in December. Lumber is shipped during the summer months, and not in December. So, that statement does not represent the correct proportion of the traffic originating in the province of Quebec. Nevertheless it goes to show that the province of Quebec supplies one-half the earnings of the Intercdlondal. Thus, for the month of December the traffic in the province of Quebec yielded $183,000, while in the provinces of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia combined it yielded $375,000: that is to say that both provinces combined yield barely as much revenue as the province of Quebec, though traffic over the branch lines is comprised in that statement. So that the province of Quebec by itself yields about one-half of the total earnings. Why then, when it comes to patronage, is she not fairly dealt with, on the basis of population?

(Translation.) Will the hon. gentleman allow me to ask him a question? The Hon. Mr. Emmerson, on May 5 last, introduced a motion to the effect that the management of the Intercolonial was unjust and oppressive for the men in the service of the Intercolonial, and did not the hon. gentleman vote against that motion?

(Translation.) I stated
at the time that, considering the lateness of the hour, I would say only a few words, reserving my right to later on address the

House at greater length and to explain the situation as I understand it. That is what I am trying to do this evening. Reverting to the province of Quebec, if it is averred that it yields one-half the total passenger and freight receipts, should it not be entitled to fair dealing at the hands of the Intercolonial management? I do not think this Government is more to blame than its predecessor in that respect, considering it is the first time I disclose how things are managed on the Intercolonial, which particulars were unknown to them. I am appealing for fairer treatment on behalf of the province of Quebec, and once these facts are disclosed, I trust the justice of our claims will be recognized.
Under the former Administration, the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Gauvreau) must have complained. Surely he must. However his complaint did not bear much fruit. For, according to the answer to my inquiry concerning the number of men employed, their names and salaries, I was given the names of forty-nine men drawing large salaries. And out of those forty-nine, how many do you think belong to the province of Quebec? Twenty, do you think, or at least, ten? You are still far astray. There are only three of those men who are from the province of Quebec. The forty-six others hail from Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and other parts.
My intention is not to speak disparagingly of our New Brunswick or Nova Scotia friends; since they are allowed to help themselves to such a large share of the booty, I cannot blame them for making the best of their opportunities. They are intelligent and shrewd, and their province can turn out as good officials as the province of Quebec; but, with all due respect to our Maritime provinces friends, I think we have in the province of Quebec as good accountants and chief clerks as they have themselves. I was anxious to disclose that condition of things and to show the situation in its true light. We are rather tired, especially in my county, of the way things are going on, and if no change is forthcoming, I for one will'not relent in my vindication of the just claims of my constituents. I shall do so more particularly for the sake of the people of Rimouski whom I have the honour to represent in this House. I have shown that we are discriminated against as regards the number of men employed. But there is another matter to which I would like to draw the attention of the minister.

(Translation.) Before the hon. gentleman passes on to another subject, may I inquire from him why he did not set a good example and express his displeasure at the action of the Government in putting out the only French-Canadian official in the employ of the Intercolonial, Mr. Caron?

hon. gentleman expects the supporters of the Government to take that stand, it must be because he is not himself plucky enough to raise his voice in protest.

(Translation.) I must say to the hon. member for Rimouski that he must have been absent from the House, or else it is quite true that there are none so deaf as those who will not hear. Mr. Gutelius has been appointed general manager of the Intercolonial, and I may state in passing that he is a perfect gentleman. I have had the pleasure of making his acquaintance. (Translation.) Does the hon. gentleman approve of the views of Mr. Gutelius?

(Translation.) The question is rather a broad one; if the hon. gentleman wishes to take it up when I am through with my remarks, I shall be glad to answer him.
I wish to refer to the circulation of trains. Far many years certain rules had been in force on the Intercolonial. On the 1st of June last the management decided to enforce the ' standard rules.' I cannot say whether the effect will be to improve the service; but I have fears that many accidents will result. I beg to call the minister's attention to the fact, hoping at the

same time that my fears will prove to be groundless. The men are called upon to familiarize themselves with new regulations; now, every change in the rules is unfortunately productive of accidents.
I am here expressing the views of the men. They would have much preferred that the old regulations with which they were all familiar had been retained, as they were perfectly safe and of a nature to protect the travelling public against all risk.
I trust that Mr. Gutelius, who is a first-rate administrator, will see to it that these regulations are only gradually enforced, in order that the men may little by little become familiar with their working, and accidents avoided.
I shall not deal at greater length with this subject, though there are many other issues that require consideration in connection with the Intercolonial. But the matter has been so much discussed by hon. gentlemen on either side, that the House must be pretty well posted in respect to the requirements of that railway.
My intention in making these remarks, as I stated a moment ago, is not to find fault with this Government any more than with the other-rather less than with the other- since we have been in power only three years; but to show to the satisfaction of the country, how the province of Quebec is being discriminated against in the matter of employment and salary. I appeal for fairer treatment, and I hope we will get it. The better paid men could be appointed from the province of Quebec in as great numbers as from the provinces of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, for, with all due respect, we have men as well qualified as they have to fill these positions. If the same facilities were offered to citizens of the province of Quebec, I am satisfied they would accept such positions with pleasure.

Mr. J, D. REID: I am sorry I do not understand the French language sufficiently well to answer my hon. friend as fully as I would like, but I shall read his speech and may be able to give him more information later. 1 understand that the hon. member claims that discrimination has been exer-

cised against the province of Quebec in the matter of selecting employees for the Intercolonial. He has stated that, out of 49 men employed in prominent positions, only three come from Quebec. He also complains that labourers employed on the Intercolonial in the province of New Brunswick are receiving $1.80 a day, while in Quebec they are only being paid $1.50. As I understand it, the track men are paid the same rate of wages all along the line, but, where additional labour is required, the employees taken on are paid at the rate prevailing in that locality in whatever province it may happen to be. In some provinces, no doubt, the rate of wages for common labour is higher than in others, and that accounts for the difference in pay of which my hon. friend has complained.
I do not believe the management of the 'Intercolonial have any intention of discriminating in any way against the province of Quebec. The hon. member has also complained that- none of the 78 employees in the dining car service come from the province of Quebec, and that only four of the 26 sleeping car conductors come from that province. It is impossible for me to answer the hon. gentleman on this point until I have a little more information, but I shall refer to the matter when the Estimates are again before the House. I understand he also complains that the Pullman conductors have to wait at Halifax instead of at Montreal. As my hon. friend knows, there are divisional points in every railway system. A train starting from a divisional point like Montreal, goes to, say, Halifax, and then comes back to Montreal, or vice versa. If Halifax is the starting point of the train, the employees would have to make their headquarters there. It matters little to the management of the Intercolonial whether these employees lay off at Montreal or Halifax, except, of course, that they must be ready to leave when the train starts. The hon. member also mentioned that some of the employees are	dissatisfied	with the
standard rules. From information I have from the management of the Intercolonial, I do not agree with the hon. member in that.	Of course, it is a
well known fact that the standard rules have been in force from Montreal to Levis for some years, and that from Levis to Moncton there has been in existence a set of rules that have grown up with the Intercolonial. I understand that the management sent out twelve or fifteen men along

the line to explain these rules to the employees, and I have heard from the leading men in the service, outside altogether of the management, that with very few exceptions the men are satisfied with the change, and feel that it is better for the service and for themselves to adopt the standard rules that are in existence on all the other railways in Canada. The management of the Intercolonial are making it as easy as possible for the employees to familiarize themselves with the new rules and pass the prescribed examination, and in the meantime the men continue in the positions they have been holding. In addition to that, the management have provided that any employees who are not able to pass, the examination shall be retained in the service in positions satisfactory to them. Every member of this House will agree with me that the men employed on the trains, where lives are at stake, must be fully qualified men. I may give a little illustration of how this examination works. A short time ago an engineer apparently in good health and strength found when he came to take the examination that he could not pass the eyesight test. Of course it would be unsafe to have a man of that kind in charge of a train for the reason that he might run past a station, and have a collision resulting in great loss of life. I only mention that to show that the standard rules and the examination in connection therewith have proved to us that certain employees are not qualified.
On account of my limited knowledge of French, I am not in a position to answer my hon. friend more fully, but, as I said before, I will read his remarks and try to give him a more complete answer at the next sitting of the House.
